Many famous actors during this era weren't able to make the transition to the talkies, and that is exactly what The Artist is about, and it does it in a very simplistic but stylized fashion. The film has been nominated for 10 Oscars, including Best Picture, Best Performance by a Lead Actor (Jean Dujardin) and a Supporting Actress (Berenice Bejo). It will probably walk away with the Best Picture title considering how appealing the subject matter is to the Academy, and how well the film was crafted. Please don't be scared off because the movie is silent or in black and white because the story is really entertaining and despite being colorless it is brighter than any other film released this year. It is really worth a watch; you won`t regret it.

The year is 1927 and George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) is at the height of his artistic career. He is a very successful Hollywood actor and producer Al Zimmer (John Goodman) is very pleased with his work. After having succeeded together yet again in a recent film, they are already collaborating for their next project. During rehearsals for their next movie, George runs into an extra named Peppy Miller (Berenice Bejo). They hit it off instantly sharing a dance number and George insists that Peppy should get the part. Pepper falls in love immediately with George, but he is married to Doris (Penelope Ann Miller) so their relationship is entirely professional. George gives Peppy the best advice she would ever receive: In order to make it in the industry she needs to be different and he paints a spot near her lip. This will be her trademark later on as she slowly begins rising to the spotlight during the arrival of the talkies. Valentin however, isn't lucky and realizes his days as a successful actor are coming to an end with the advent of these talking pictures. People want to see new faces and hear their voices. Al Zimmer realizes this and breaks relations with George, so Valentin decides to produce, direct, and star in his own silent film. The movie is a failure as people want to see these new talkies, and as Valentin`s fame becomes to decline, Peppy Miller begins to grow into a superstar. Valentin is left with nothing except his faithful driver, Clifton (James Cromwell) and his Jack Russell Terrier named Jack. The times have changed for the great artists and fortunes are reversed.

The Artist is among my top ten favorite films of the year and it works really well, not only as homage to these silent films, but as a love story as well. Along with Midnight in Paris, these are perhaps the two best romantic movies of the year and would make for an excellent date. I`ve already mentioned some of the technical aspects, but now I would like to praise the performances from Jean Dujardin, Berenice Bejo, and the dog (which was played in most part by Uggie). I can`t leave out the dog, because he plays an important role in this film, and in a way is Valentin`s faithful companion and savior. Jean Dujardin does deserve the Oscar nomination for his performance, he was terrific, and I think I enjoyed it over George Clooney`s. If he wins, it will be well deserved. My favorite performance of the film however, comes from Berenice Bejo, who was also nominated as a supporting actress. She is just terrific and shines every time she`s on screen. Her performance gives this black and white movie a lot of color. Both Bejo and Dujardin have worked together with director Hazanavicius in the past in the French spy spoof film OSS 117. I`ve never seen the movie, nor its sequel, but after seeing The Artist I`m very much interested in doing so. Overall this is a terrific film and one you won`t want to miss.

A rapturously entertaining and emotional love letter to cinema, creativity, and romance, The Artist says more with no dialogue than the rest of the talky Best Picture nominees combined. Calling it a masterwork of pure motion picture artistry would be as gross an understatement as saying talkies might someday replace silent movies in the '20s. Aping everything from Douglas Fairbanks to Citizen Kane to Singin' in the Rain, this superb piece of filmmaking is edifying from its letter-perfect performances right to its beautifully lensed homage to classic H'Wood. To put it in a single title card: joyous filmgoing.

In this PG-13-rated black and white silent dramedy, an up-and-coming H'Wood bit player (Bejo) falls for a moving picture superstar (Dujardin) just as the advent of talkies changes the business.

This reviewer has seen the future and, thankfully, it's the past. 8 years ago, when he made his own love letter to silent and Golden Age comedies, he ran out of money to fully realize it as a black and white title carded kiss to classic H'Wood. Ironically, work began last fall to finish this vision, but writer/director Michael Hazanavicius has truly crafted as perfect an idol as any film fan could hope to make, assembling the ridiculously talented likes of Dujardin and Bejo to give brilliant unspoken lip service to a trailblazing era of filmmaking. The sure-to-be Oscar hat trick is that his film is far more than an homage--it hangs in its own gallery, a heartfelt masterpiece that's not just a piece of throwback pop art.

Bottom line: The gold rush.

Where should I start? Well, the plot revolves around famous silent-film actor George Valentin (Jean Dujardin). Soon, however, the birth of "talkie-films", make Valentin's films look out of style, and he himself, is looked at as a has-been. On top of that, a little extra actress named, Peppy Miller (Berenice Bejo) who Valentin helped get her career started, becomes a sensational actress in the new talkies, and all her films put Valentin's to shame. Now this is not a new story, its been told before, but The Artist does it perfectly well. We see the emotional struggle through his frustrations, we see how he loses his friends and family, how desperate he is just to survive, but what he really wants is for his name to survive. No one appreciates his creative storytelling anymore, because people want a change, but Valentin prefers to keep things the ways they are, and as a result, rejects change, only to suffer. Mr Dujardin does an incredible job with this role, and in my opinion, he deserves an award. This is because he is required to act through his movements and facial features. He cannot rely on his voice in any ways, he has to express his state of mind through his face, and that can be very difficult. This movie is a terrific homage to the classic silent films of the 20's, it really looks authentic. Even the opening credits look identical to the opening credits of an old 20's or 30's movie. It has always been a dream of mine to see something like this in theaters. I grew up with old movies, and some of them were silent films (A Trip To The Moon, Phantom of The Opera, Nosferatu, ect.), they possessed a magical charm that made the movie feel a lot like an actual story being told. True, you don't hear what people have to say, but the audience is smart enough to figure out what is going on, without dialogue. An example could be when Valentin is drunk at the bar (We know he is drunk because his clothes are messy, he's holding a bottle, and he's sees little people speaking to him). When he sees a miniature version of himself shouting at him, the audience can tell that the tiny Valentin is scolding the actual Valentin for his childish and immature behavior. In the end, The Artist is a remarkable film, and a great tribute to classic silent films. That's not to say it's perfect, but there is very little wrong with it. It's a simple story, which some could say is a bit disappointing, but I left the theatre satisfied with what I saw. The Artist gets 4 1/2 movie cameras out of 5.

It would be easy for modern audiences to dismiss "The Artist."  As a tribute to the cinema of old--very, very old--not only is it black and white, but it's also almost entirely silent.  This may sound unappealing to a generation raised on bright colors, loud noises and special effects, but you will be doing yourself a great disservice if you refuse to see this movie because of such quibbles.  "The Artist" is a wonderful film: entertaining, funny, moving, poignant, everything you could want in a movie such as this.  Yes, it's basically a modern silent film, but somehow it doesn't feel like a gimmick.  It would work even if there was sound throughout (though admittedly it may lose some of its charm).

George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) is the biggest movie star in the late 1920s.  With his dashing good looks and dazzling smile, he simply lights up the screen.  His exciting adventure tales are popular, he has many fans, and he lives in a beautiful mansion in Hollywood.  Life is good.  But things take a dramatic turn when he learns that his studio is going to start making movies with sound ("talkies," as they come to be called), and his services would no longer be required.  When the "talkies" become immensely popular, the public's interest in George drops rapidly.  As he's reminded by the studio head (John Goodman), he's a product of a different time; he's associated with so-called "silent films"; no one wants to hear him speak.

The studio's new darling is Peppy Miller (Berenice Bejo), a perky young starlet who actually got her start as an extra in one of George's films before breaking out when the "talkie" films became big.  She actually owes much of her stardom to George, who came up with the idea of penciling in a beauty mark on her cheek, to differentiate her from other actresses.  The budding friendship/relationship between these two different performers makes up the backbone of the film.

As is the case with the silent films of old, the plot is simple, but that doesn't mean it's not effective.  And although there's not much complication to the storyline, you certainly can't say it's easy on the actors.  Watching Dujardin, Bejo, and the rest of the cast, you really get a newfound appreciation for the silent era film stars.  It had to be exceedingly difficult to perform with such little dialogue (yes, we can see the characters speak, but title cards were used sparingly, basically only to progress the story).  Character development had to be done mostly through expressions, mannerisms, and body language.  Remarkably we still get a very good sense of George and Peppy's characters, and Dujardin and Bejo both received well-earned Oscar nominations.

"The Artist" also works as a bit of an historical piece.  The rather dismissive reaction George gets from the studios was commonplace for actors who were hot stuff during the silent era, but couldn't quite make the transition to the "talkies."  As we saw in the classic musical "Singin' in the Rain" (1952), there were instances in which a popular silent performer's voice just wouldn't work in movies with sound.  We discover that George is a Frenchman, so he likely was told the same thing.  It had to be disheartening to be so popular in the movies at one point, and then, seemingly overnight, to be declared irrelevant.  George struggles with the concept of sound itself throughout the movie, most cleverly illustrated in a dream sequence.

"The Artist" has been nominated for 10 Oscars and is currently the front runner for Best Picture, and that's encouraging as this may cause some potential viewers to seek it out.  It's a great movie that works on several levels, and I implore you not to be so shallow as to ignore it based on its nostalgic qualities.  You'll miss out on a wonderful experience.

As a film on it's own, The Artist is a charming, endearing, and enjoyable throwback to the classic silent film era. But as an actual homage of silent films of yesteryear, The Artist is a rather uncomfortable experience with muddled awkwardness, and an inherently vague lead character. The film will feel thoroughly enchanting to most moviegoers, but I feel it's only the real silent film buffs who will feel that the experience is slightly off-putting. The problem relies in it's very medium. It claims to be an homage to silent films but in turn, it feels like it just sits on the border between homage and parody. There are several scenes that feel odd and jerky, scenes that almost poke fun at very similar films of the age, scenes like: the melodramatic discovery of Valentin's things in Peppy's house, the hallucination at the bar, and the "genius dog." The end result feels strange and oddly humorous (which is most probably unintentional). The parallels in the storyline are rather clever and amusing, but it falls apart in these scenes. Something else that adds to the film's unraveling rely in the lead character, George Valentin. I was very intrigued about the central conflict, a silent film star struggling to adjust to the norms of the industry. But it's central conflict ends up to be something much more shallow and silly. Instead of a story about the struggles of an ever-changing society (which would have been marvelous), the story ends up being about a pompous, selfish, proud douche-bag that's very hard to care about (which is uninteresting). If you take this film as you see it, or just watch it without over-thinking, you will enjoy yourself. The storytelling is invigorating, the score is incredible, the performances are great, and the entire plot is amusing and fun. It's only when you dissect film and study it as an homage, that you realize it is flawed and rather disappointing. In a way, it's a shallow ordinary Hollywood film that's aiming to be accessible to contemporary moviegoers (and it succeeds.) And in that same way, it's great because it's a film that many people will enjoy and may possibly attract new fans to the silent film genre. But in another way, The Artist almost feels like an insult to the intelligence and taste of silent film fans. Overall, it's a fun and enjoyable film, but it's flaws and faults as a silent film homage may be distracting to some, but not so much that it detracts greatly from the experience. But it's flaws result in the film becoming more ordinary and less unique, more forgettable and less memorable.

In a similar spirit to Scorcese's 'Hugo', The Artist celebrates the early years of cinema by paying homage to the style of the silent era. Whereas Scorsese made deliberate use of 3D technology, to celebrate the original master of special effects Georges Melies, The Artist goes in the opposite direction by opting for academy ratio, black & white visuals and an almost silent experience. 

This is French made, though set in 'Hollywoodland'. You may recognize John Goodman & James Cromwell, but the leads Jean Dujardin & Berenice Bejo are unknowns which just adds to the feeling that you are watching something a bit different from the usual Hollywood flick. This is a very likeable and enjoyable movie experience and a welcome reprieve from the excessive sonic booming of modern movies. It's good to be reminded of how powerful cinema can still be working within the boundaries of the old technology.

Despite being more than just a novelty picture, nobody's expecting a new wave of 'silent' movies to spring forth. While it's good fun to be educated in the old ways, no-one's going to be ditching surround sound anytime soon. And just one more thing - there's never been any such thing as a 'silent' movie. Even back in the day there was always a musical accompaniment & in some respects this is the advantage modern 'talkies' have over 'silent' cinema. At least the music can be turned off! No such luck in the Artist which has a soundtrack that starts to become overbearing. That's the only thing that annoyed me, but still a film that has to be seen.
If there was ever a silent film to watch in your entire life, this would definitely be the one to see.

Yes, it's true.  The picture that has garnered the second most Oscar nominations is a silent picture.  Unconventional, to say the least, but certainly a welcome shake-up.  However, in the age of cutting edge effects, filming technique, and, well, sound, it's might be kind of surprising that this little film is receiving all the adulation.  Is it because critics are in love with the simplicity of the film, or is it because they generally abhor all things that the public likes (and that Michael Bay can deliver)?  Well, honestly, it's a bit of both.  The film is a throwback to yesteryear in nearly every way, but it's nostalgic qualities are not merely Oscar prostitution.  
George Valentin (French actor and Best Actor frontrunner Jean Dujardin) is a bona fide movie star - a silent movie star, that is.  He's at the top of his game.  Audiences adore him, and he has almost everything a man could ever want.  Then something odd happens.  A chance run-in with a beautiful would-be actress, Peppy Miller (French actress and Best Supporting Actress nominee Berenice Bejo), upends George.  He's drawn to her captivating beauty, and her charming personality.  Then the unthinkable happens.  His studio bosses tell him that they are moving into production of "talkies" - movies with actors voices and sounds besides music.  George says he won't do them, and sets out to continue making silent pictures on his own.  As fate would have it, Peppy becomes a star in the new format.  As George's world crumbles, Peppy's career soars.  The two seem to reverse roles, but still have a connection, despite being worlds apart.  
From the top down, this film is a meticulously-crafted work of art.  Most of the credit rightly should go to French writer/director Michel Hazanavicius who has taken a great deal of care to create something that hold reverent the silent film, but also make something that modern audiences can appreciate.  Whether Hazanavicius merely reveres the silent film or it's an obsession of his could be a point of debate, but what's undeniable is the entertaining aspect of the film.  The story is quant, but endearing, yet despite its old-school wholesomeness (besides an unnecessary and seemingly out of place gesture), there's a bit of a dark element to it as well.  Plus, there are several scenes that a just flat out funny.  Who says that a movie has to be crude or profane?  Physical comedy and some self-awareness still go a long way in making people smile.  
As demure as it may be to say that the acting is first rate, you can't really deny the appeal of both Dujardin and Bejo (even if they are French).  They both have charisma that is almost unheard of - pun intended - in today's cinema.  Both have enough emotion in their facial expressions to pull off their silent film characters with ease.  Besides the leads, Hazanavicius has included small roles for the likes of John Goodman (The Princess and the Frog) and James Cromwell (Secretariat), as well as bit parts for Missi Pyle (Spring Breakdown) and Malcolm McDowell (Easy A).  All the actors work well within the framework of the silent film, but Dujardin and Bejo are clearly the standouts.  That is, except for the adorable dog, Uggy.  He's quite a character himself.  However, their characters probably wouldn't have the personality were it not for the ever-present score from frequent Hazanavicius collaborator Ludovic Bource.  His broad-ranging compositions help ground the characters, as well as give them a unique personality.    
It's easy to assume that this movie is simply Oscar bait, and to a degree, those assumptions are accurate.  However, what those assumptions don't take into account is the overwhelming affection the cast and crew have for the silent cinema features of yesteryear.  It's easy to make a movie in black and white to give a film an old-school feel, but how many filmmakers do you know nowadays who can capture humor, emotion, and a competent story without audible dialogue?  Dujardin and Bejo are great in their roles, and Hazanavicius really knows the ins and outs of silent filmmaking - be it a reverence for the tactics, or possibly an obsession.  The end result is a satisfying cinematic experience, and one that probably deserves the buzz it's getting - if, for no other reason, it's unique.

The true thrill of The Artist is that while it stands alone as a prime example of quality film-making and old-fashioned story-telling, it will also encourage a new generation of film fans to explore the wonders of early cinema, thereby ensuring the greats of yesteryear are not forgotten. If this doesn't win plenty of Oscars it will be an outright robbery - and here's hoping that Hollywood doesn't squander Dujardin and Bejo in forgettable projects in the wake of the success of this winning, playful cinematic triumph.

Considering that there was a rather unorthodox and unique idea behind it with a black and white silent film set in the 1920s being released in 2011, The Artist still provided us with the thought that it could become something that'll renovate the birth of cinema, so to speak. With this in mind and having said that it is surrounded by all these colourful Hollywood dramas, action and science fiction films that we see in this generation, everything about The Artist literally swept away not only every film released in 2011 but the majority of the films released over the past decade! It has it all: it's charming to watch with strong bonds between the characters, it is very emotional, it was surprisingly very funny with a lot of brilliant jokes and most of all: it manages to successfully capture the reality of the time setting. To be able to pull off a successful silent film in this generation is a very difficult task considering that we are now piled with films with extremely high budgets featuring various aspects such as overloading visual effects, action films and the re-birth of 3D. So, having said this, there would need to be a solid enough story for it to work. Quite frankly, for it to perhaps reboot the older world of cinema it had to be a movie about movies otherwise if it's part of any other particular theme of film story-wise, it wouldn't really be something that hadn't been repeated time and time again. Unlike many films in most recent years, The Artist consists of many breakthrough scenes that are somewhat referenced to Citizen Kane by Orson Welles and will undoubtedly become landmark scenes in many years to come. French actor Jean Dujardin portrays English 'speaking' actor George Valentin and gives quite possibly one of the best performances in a very long time! Dujardin's approach to the character very closely resembles both Clark Gable's masterful performance as Rhett Butler in Gone With The Wind back in 1939 and Gene Kelly's witty and delightful role as Don Lockwood in classic 1952 musical Singin' In The Rain due to their mutually charming nature particularly towards the opposing gender. In addition to the mesmerizing attributes, Dujardin bought forth a lot of witty comedy that not only had similarity with Gene Kelly, but also with the legendary Charlie Chaplin in his films. Dujardin rightfully deserves the Academy Award for Best Leading Actor for renovating the silent style of acting and defining its true meaning so exquisitely. Alongside Dujardin comes another breakthrough performance from French actress Bérénice Bejo who brings forth a Marilyn Monroe-like character Peppy Miller with a naturally young and sexy nature, so to speak, who adds passion and pure enjoyment to the story. The bond that Valentin and Miller have is beyond any other romantic connection between a male and female protagonist seeing as there's a very low supply of passionate kissing or intimate sexual contact. So, there's an immediate bond between them and proves that emotional bonds are the most important aspect within relationships. Dujardin and Bejo together introduce a brand new message about acting that action really does speak louder than words. In the supporting cast are various American and British actors featuring the likes of James Cromwell as Valentin's valet, John Goodman as Al Zimmer - head of Kinograph Studios who Valentin regularly worked with in his silent projects, Penelope Ann Miller as Valentin's wife and a cameo appearance from A Clockwork Orange actor Malcolm McDowell in a role simply known as "The Butler". Another piece of treasure in the ensemble cast is to Uggie as Jack, who's a trained Jack Russell Terrier who has appeared in various projects over the years (most recently in Water For Elephants). Hats go off to this dog who adds a lot of witty comedy to the film alongside Jean Dujardin and also a sense of innocence that'll guarantee to gain the film a wider audience despite its occasionally unappealing style of film to many others out there. Uggie's "performance" brings forth that emotionally realistic role that we saw so amazingly from Joey in War Horse! With the majority being French behind all of the production aspects, they could not have accomplished a more accurate setting with the world of American Hollywood and restored the category of silent films so amazingly! In addition to the traditional 1.33:1 ratio of filming that was used during the silent era, the use of classical music composed by Ludovic Bource adds more liveliness and enchantment to the film as it tells the story alongside the actions from characters directed magnificently by Michel Hazanavicius. Hazanavicius provides numerous styles of direction during The Artist that feature upbeat and rather passionate forms including dancing and acting from the films within The Artist, the use of the background settings and directing Uggie but more depressingly, the personal psychological pain presented. His script was absolutely magnificent as well and became another characteristic expressed that provides the fact that films are really about actions rather than words. Overall, The Artist is truly a masterpiece for the ages that will leave you speechless in every single way! It's not only a love story between a man and a woman but it's also and most importantly a love story about motion pictures. You could literally name many classic films (both silent and sound) where The Artist can in one way or another numerously be compared to. It's a miraculous achievement in French cinema and tributes the works from filmmakers part of the silent era that include Charlie Chaplin, Georges Méliès, Howard Hawks and perhaps to Mel Brooks too for his work in the 1976 silent satirical comedy Silent Movie. The upcoming 84th Academy Awards and the majority of the awards presented would deservedly belong to The Artist due to the impact it has had in the world of cinema.

When I heard there was a silent movie in theaters, I knew it was something I had to see. Not since Raza and I viewed "The Birth of a Nation" has a silent film been so hyped. Naturally, I donned by bow tie, red pants, and navy blazer, greased my hair back and did the Charleston down to the old cinema as I did in 1927. 

There are many things I could talk about when it comes to this film, but for length's sake, I will keep it short. First, it was the epitome of irony. Right? I mean, here I am in 2011, typing this from my iPhone, seeing a silent film about the death of silent films. Critics have dubbed this the beginning of a new era in silent film making, yet this movie highlighted how it came to a fiery end all thanks to the Great Depression! The biggest disappointment I had with this positive was that I did not wear plaid to the theater. Shame on me for not researching.

Second was, this was the anti-Michael Bay. It was a quiet, simple and had a straightforward plot that made sense to boot. All of these things are the polar opposites of Michael Bay films. The only similarly came in the house fire scene, but in a Bay movie, the house would've exploded, destroyed the whole neighborhood and caused the mass extinction of humans in the area. 

Third, it was silent. Silent can be good. Often when I go see movies, I leave them thinking "I could've written a better script than that." Here, I could make up my own lines and actually enjoy them. And you know what? I did just that, which enhanced my movie viewing experience! Another plus. 

Finally, it was all movie genres in one. I saw a comedy, rom-com, drama, horror and action film all rolled into one. My ticket may have been $10, but I saw $50 worth of movie! That is a movie I can get behind!

I am giving The Artist 4 out of 5 stars due to the complains above, and it lacking the two things I need most in cinema: sex and violence. I also felt it would be ironic to give it 4 stars given my average rating for Michael Bay films is 2 stars. See the irony? Yeah, I don't either...

Although being presented in black and white, The Artist was actually produced in colour, with modern cameras and lenses. For me this really brought the film down. There is hardly any grain throughout of the film, and even a few zoom shots. Overall I still highly recommend this, as it is very enjoyable to watch and as I said earlier "An excellent homage to the "silent era" of cinema."

This movie is absolutely incredible  that celebrates what we all love about movies, but in this case and, obviously, most specifically, silent cinema. I can't really say enough good things about this movie, it continually gets better and I was actually kind of sad when the movie ended because I'd have liked to see it go longer. What holds this movie back for me personally, though, is the nature of the film itself:  It's largely silent.  Yes, there's a score underneath.  But it's not engaging, just as it's not engaging to try to read an actor's lips or read a title card that says what the actor just said.  Granted, you can pretty much guess what the actors say most of the time because their physical performances are so strong, and as a writer, I both understand and appreciate the different directions the script takes.

But bottom line for me:  A good movie engages an audience.  I admire and understand The Artist but never feel truly engaged in the world presented to me.  I fully understand the film's message--that silent films can still move people just as much as talkies (And anyone who knows me or has seen my shorts know I've only done non-dialogue pieces, and I love the notion of showing, not telling in films.)--I strongly feel that this is a step backwards.  I fully realize this film has huge, huge fans who idolize everything within its 1 hour and 40 minutes runtime, but in my personal opinion, this is film wouldn't be lauded as highly if it had dialogue. A unique silent film concerning the business of silent films, and how one megawatt talent (Jean Dujardin) experiences the changing of times as his once prominent career is thrust into oblivion as a talent he helped along the way (Berenice Bejo) starts to see her career explode, and how the two remain connected. This movie is part satire on the industry, but it is largely a dark, unsettling look at a former titan whose ego and life take a pounding. The fact that director Michel Hazanavicius makes this movie so moving, being we actually care about these characters and how they will end up, is an enormous feat to pull off being that no words are spoken largely throughout this picture. Through a simple score, gorgeous cinematography, and Oscar-caliber turns from both Dujardin and Bejo, "The Artist" is a good motion picture. Some critics say it is "just another silent movie" and it is largely unnecessary, but I disagree. Maybe not deserving of the "Best Picture" award it got, but this film possesses a sort of darkness and somberness many silent films would never entertain, as largely the business was all fun and games, mostly concentrated on the slapstick antics of both Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton. This film goes to dark places, which is surprising, but it pays off in the end.

It's rare to say that a movie is unlike anything you've ever seen but The Artist is just such a movie.  Never before have I felt as if I had somehow stepped into a time machine in such a way as while watching this film.  It just oozes visual mastery over it's subject matter and theme.  The Artist is a black and white silent film about the time period during the late 1920's and early 1930's when Hollywood transitioned from being a silent film industry into a talking one.  For some stars, that was not a smooth transition.  

This is the premise of the film as we follow the downfall of an omega star in silent Hollywood as he fails to grip the change in the winds.  I just have to say that I absolutely love this movie!  Everything from the performances, the flawless direction, the look of the film and the spot on orchestrated music has been lovingly crafted to fit the movie perfectly.  This was obviously someone's dream project and it shows.  I was enthralled from beginning to end and that is no easy feat considering that there aren't any lines of spoken dialogue in the first 96 minutes of the film.  

Enough cannot be said about the stunning and charming acting here.  Jean Dujardin and Berenice Bejo' have created characters that come alive on screen.  I especially appreciated Bejo's portrayal of a starlet named Peppy Miller.  Every time she was on screen I found my eyes drifting toward her.  She has been nominated for best supporting actress for this role and will probably lose out to Octavia Spencer (who was excellent in The Help) but I feel as though Bejo' had easily one of my favorite performances of the year.  

All in all, although I adore the Artist, I cannot honestly recommend it to quite everyone.  If you have a closed mind, an inability to be charmed, or do not want to see an amazingly original film, then this movie is not for you.  Everyone else, follow my advice and see this film as soon as possible.

Synopsis:  This modern-day silent film recounts the poignant end of the silent-movie era in the late 1920s. The story contrasts the declining fortunes of a silent-screen superstar with his lover's rise to popularity as a darling of the "talkies."

Truly great film's are not great simply by their own merits, the timing in the release more often than not has a huge impact on their immediate evaluation and how they are viewed decades after their initial run through cinemas have stalled.  If Star Wars were released in 1987 instead of 1977, it's likely it would have not been nearly as acclaimed or culturally significant.  Time is an important aspect in filmmaking.  

When it comes to The Artist, it's clear the film could have been made at no other time.  Though the picture has the same style as a classic silent film, it's far from the same look.  The cinematography (like all contemporary films) draws on the works of countless directors of photography from years gone by, and it's gorgeous, and in no way remotely resembles the films of yore.  The script, clearly wishes for it's audience to be entertained rather than bog them down with preachy statements of the nostalgia of ol' yesteryear, and instead plays with it's modern-day audience's perceptions of silent films with wit and intelligence.

At the heart of the picture though are it's two leads.  Jean Dujardin and Bérénice Bejo give tremendously warm performances that infect the entire picture, when Jean smiles the entire room smiles with him, when Berenice weeps, the film weeps, not only are the performances incredible, they're essential to the film, as much as the score and direction.  

Presented in Black and white in the old 4:3 aspect ratio, The Artist is a warm and witty tribute to the films of yesteryear.

Nods to several classic films, though I see a story arc which makes The Artist a cross between Sullivan's Travels & A Star is Born. I give The Artist several points for superb acting, and for the impressive technique shown in making a modern-day homage to cinema history. The story is old and cliche, which was especially disappointing given how well the other aspects of the movie came together. I feel like Hazanavicius got so excited about making a silent movie and all the technical aspects and classic movie references that involved that he decided the story itself could be phoned in.

The Artist review
2011's most critically acclaimed film (97% on Rotten Tomatoes!) "The Artist" arrives to much fanfare (it's currently the Oscar frontrunner for best picture) but does it live up to hype? In a nutshell, I would have to say no. It is a charming and nostalgic film but it is hamstrung by its dependence on its silent film aesthetic.

The film follows silent-film star George Valentino ( Jean Dujardin). He is an artist at the peak of his powers; he is adored by audiences and loved by critics. But the film world is changing and the introduction of sound is just around the corner.  George is reluctant to take place in these "talkies", as he thinks that they are just a fad; he is forced with a choice, change with the times or be left behind.  To complicate matters even further, George feels a connection to Peppy Miller, an actress rising through the ranks, but is George's world big enough for two stars, let alone one that stars in "talkies"?
 
Jean Dujardin is brilliant as George. He cuts a dashing figure with his pencil-thin moustache and slick- backed hair. He captures a real range of emotions with his mannerisms and does his silent-film predecessors proud. The sight of him beaming his mega-watt smile in a tuxedo will undoubtedly become one of modern cinemas most recognizable images. Berenice Bejo offers great support as Peppy Miller; she nails the wide eyed optimism of the idealistic young starlet and is a great counterpoint to George's reclusive egoism. The rest of the cast is rounded out by predominately American actors who look like the personification of their profession: John Goodman plays a studio mogul, Penelope Ann Miller is a glamorous housewife and James Cromwell a loyal butler.
             
"The Artist" does not just pay homage to silent films; it is in itself a silent film. This fact alone I imagine will turn off quite a large amount of modern cinema audiences. It is a daunting prospect for people raised on ear- splitting THX-sound to sit through a film that only has two lines of dialogue and is largely sound effect free. It may seem uncultured and incurious for someone to dismiss this film on those terms (I didn't), but I must admit I found the soundlessness disquieting. There is a reason these films are extinct, they have been made redundant by modern technique. I would have loved an amalgamation of old and new techniques; why not have Georges film silent, but have him talking behind the scenes. Alas, that is not what "The Artist" is. I also felt that despite some clever parts the film lacked inventiveness. I had hoped that this would be like a Pixar film; blending nostalgia and feeling into something superlative. But director Michel Hazanavicius is so concerned with his gimmick that he occasionally forgets to stimulate the audience.

I thought that the celebration of cinema was done far better in Martin Scorsese's "Hugo". Both films are nominated for Oscars this year and that leads me to a strange point; "The Artist" is my least favourite film out of the nine nominees (I haven't seen "Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close").  I would literally rather see eight films win over "The Artist". In its purest definition this is a (relatively) low budget, silent, French film. Which is a great experiment but I'm not exactly sure how it has got the awards momentum it has. I know that the academy loves an underdog, but Best Picture? 

Despite my criticisms "The Artist" is a nice film. It has great performances and charm to spare, and I admire (but don't love) it for its adherence to bygone ideas. There a lot of people that will be won over wholeheartedly by this film, unfortunately I was not one of them.

Having watched this soon-to-be Oscar winner in the local cinema (after repeatedly brainwashed by its trailer in the multiplexes), indeed it's my third encounter with silent films behind SUNRISE (1927), and FINANCES OF THE GRAND DUKE (1924). The film is masterfully presented from the very beginning until the NEAR-end. THE ARTIST is among the laureates of 2011's film territory without any doubt.

But, in my very own opinion, the much-anticipated Oscar sweep is simply a victory of nostalgia. If it had been made decades before, say 60 years ago, it would be boosted as a silent version of A STAR IS BORN with an excellent cast and splendid score, smooth and melodic, and be ascertained as a major contender but with little likeness to procure the sure-fire ultimate winner kudos which it has now in 2012, when audience has been accustomed to talkies for ages. THE ARTIST is defying all the regular habits to remind cineastes that a silent B&W film could be so potently entertaining and watchable. My point is that I don't think the film itself should take all the credit, though the team behind does have a genius concoction to evoke the retro fixation to its core targets, film-related mass which are the pillar of the film industry (academy included for sure). I doubt who in the field will not love the film? It's a crowd-pleaser for filmmakers, especially the elderly rank. (Actually THE ARTIST and HUGO are holding the same slant here, but Martin Scorsese utilizes tons of money to invest a monolithic fantasy while a foreign no-name Michel Hazanavicius and his troupe achieves the same effect through a more lightweight and unconventional approach, so if the ballots are leaning towards THE ARTIST, no one should scratch their heads.)

Also another edge of THE ARTIST is that despite of the pungent situation of both film's languid box office income is embarrassing no matter who will win the game eventually, there is an essential difference between them, that is THE ARTIST has no difficulty to retrieve its meager budget ($15,000,000), meanwhile HUGO seems to be on the right track of becoming another commercial flunk like THE GOLDEN COMPASS (if not more) even though it's a Scorsese vehicle, which is not an encouraging exemplar for Hollywood tycoons to bankroll their future projects. 

Digressing back from the film itself, Jean Dujardin is my current winning for BEST ACTOR, whose protean flair of balancing between comedy and drama is admirable and compelling; Ms. Bejo's ambiguous leading/supporting status maybe hamper her ballots but she is impeccable in the film. 

The said "NEAR-end" incident concerns my thought of the final scene of the talkie moment, which is a regretful anticlimax for me (although sound and words are plied flawlessly during the middle session to underline the conversion to the talkie era), but Mr. Dujardin's French accent last word is not attuned with his character at all, which downgrades the film as well.

Anyway, I could have rated the film higher, but my heart goes with HUGO, but who cares?

George Valentin (Dujardin) is one of the most popular silent-film actors, and is loved by almost everybody that attends movies. All of that changes when the talkies come around in 1929 however. Missing the chance to soon become a talkies star due to his sense of pride, George ends up losing everything, leading him to multiple suicide attempts. But the movies' newest star Peppy Miller (Bejo), who once played an extra on a Valentin flick, has loved the guy ever since they first met-- and this causes her to try and start his career up again. Earlier, I've said that "Beginners" was my favorite movie of 2011, but that all changed the second that I saw "The Artist". A silent-film that is all about the end of silent films, (the year silent films ended) the movie plays out in such an old fashioned way, which is so beautiful to see-- it seems society likes to watch car chases and explosions rather than art, and it's good to see that somebody cares. Filmed in sumptuous black-and-white, and done with limited dialogue, "The Artist" is original, authentic, and engaging, but what I think is the coolest thing is that this film really would've only worked as a silent film. I'm glad that director Michel Hazanavicius realized this, he is for sure a director I'll be looking out for. He creates a world that I didn't want to leave, truly proving that the movies still aren't hopeless. The actors too, shine so bright here, with Dujardin who will surely be hard to beat at the Oscars, and with Bejo proving herself to be the new Marion Cotillard. Their isn't a flaw in "The Artist"; it's just so good to see that the lost world of silent films isn't yet gone. Highly recommended.

In an age where Hollywood is heading in the direction of big, bloated 3D blockbusters, The Artist reflects on where we were almost a century ago. What was film like back then? In a very unique stylistic choice, French filmmaker Michel Hazanavicius decides to give the audience the silent film treatment. And yet, this style is very much a way of identifying with the main protagonist, George Valentin.
Valentin is the most popular actor of his time. He is a proud man - too proud - but his films make money and audiences love him. That is, until the day that the studios decide to introduce sound into the process. As Valentin is told in a board meeting, audiences loved his face, but they won't love his voice. His days are over - out with the old, in with the new. As his life begins to crumble, a young actress named Peppy Miller replaces Valentin as the most in demand. Interesting enough, Peppy developed a friendship with George prior to his firing. 
The Artist is a pleasant film, a reflection on a time when sound - something we all take for granted now in watching movies - was completely controversial, threatening to destroy the lives of many established actors and changing the face of Hollywood forever. Today, the evolution of 3D has reached the same level of controversy, and once again seems to be changing the way we will continue to watch movies. In times like these, it's important to reflect on the past.
I admire Jean Dujardin and Berenice Bejo, who play George and Peppy respectively. They embrace the camera with the same kind of screen presence as Charlie Chapman or Lillian Gish. The soundtrack is equally exquisite, and is a key attribute to invoking the emotional arcs that this story travels through. Yet as much as I enjoyed The Artist, I am weary of the accolades this film is receiving. I don't think it's anywhere near the same league as Singin' In The Rain, still in my opinion the best film ever made about the transition towards "talkies". I find The Artist's story a bit predictable and rather shallow. What saves it for me is the style. In an age where every studio film has sucked the life out of the magic of visual effects, The Artist is wonderfully refreshing, breathing new life and new perspective into a dormant art form.

One minute leading man is buying his wife an expensive gift because he's afraid his wife will be mad about an innocent picture. Next minute he's cheating on her...then she disappears and doesn't even attend the auction of her own estate. I was able to predict the twists of this movie every step of the way. The only reason it's not totally forgetable is because it was in black and white. Without that it just becomes a contrived and silly version of "A Star is Born."

"The Artist": 8.5/10. Michel Hazanavicius's black-and-white silent film about, what else, the transition from the mass production of silent films in the late 1920s to "talkies", or sound films. Set in 1927, Jean Dujardin portrays silent film star George Valentin who is filled with dread as his livelihood is put in jeopardy. At the same time, rising star Peppy Miller (Berenice Bejo) is more or less guaranteed to become a juggernaut of a film star. Without giving too much away, "The Artist" tells the story of their interlocking fates (or destinies). 

Getting right to it, this novelty film, while well made, does not thrive itself on technical cinematic excellence, but, instead, is fueled with pure joy and is unabashedly a crowd-pleaser. And I am talking about a GOOD crowd-pleaser, not one built on cheap tear-jerking moments and cheesy humor. Hazanavicius handles the direction quite well especially in a scene in which Valentin, amongst a group of talking people, cannot speak, but the film's stars, Dujardin and Bejo are the biggest reasons why "The Artist" plays as well as it does. In the end, it is impressive that anyone could get away with a black-and-white silent film in the 21st century, but it has been done. Although, for all of its exuberance, it left me a little cold. It is not vapid by any means, but the character's could use some more depth and, as a whole, "The Artist" is a little too lightweight, but it is well worth seeing, preferably in a movie theater.

Its not a period film. It's a comment on art forms and popularity of a particular art form; influence of technology on acting and cinema on the whole and finally love and appreciation for a 'great artist'. In this case, it was Hollywood between late 1920s and early 1930s, the time when a great transition took place from silent movies to talkies. Excellent acting by both Jean Dujardin and Berenice Bejo. For me personally, The Artist is the film that I have been wanting for a very long time and it has been well worth the wait. If you are someone who loves cinema at all, then you must make it your duty to see this film. As a film geek, one of my favorite things to talk about is silent cinema. It is obvious to see that the way films were first made and now are drastically different. But like all things, we need to be reminded of what we have done and where we have come from. The end result is a film that is not only entertaining and gorgeous, but shockingly touching and just a dream to view. That is the best way for me to describe this film: watching a dream. Here is the thing: I personally love black and white cinema. Quoting film critic Roger Ebert, black and white has a certain quality to it, less realistic and more dream like. With a film that has a story as traditional as what The Artist has, if this film was in color it would ruin the entire experience. Same with there being no dialogue at all until the very end. During this film, you are with George Valentine (Jean Dujardin) as he has to deal with the feeling of the art he loved starts to change. And what an experience it is. If there is one other reason that is overlooked about this film, it would be that the message of the film is heavily overlooked. The main message of this film is that art is always changing and while it is nice to stick with the type of art you adore, we as humans need to adapt to new types, embrace how they are, and find the true beauty in every variation. Just like George in this film, he hates talking cinema, seeing as how he was one of the leaders of the golden silent age. But, naturally, he learns to love talking in films after he has a few... events that happen to him. He tries so hard to keep things the way they are, that he soon blocks everything out and when he is introduced to new ideas, he starts to go slightly mad. With that transition, I am in love with the direction of this film. Michel Hazanavicius does a wonderful job setting up the film and making us fall into this world. There is a thing with modern audiences in that they can't stand silent films, they hate black and white. To the average film goer, what they require is strong sex appeal, huge special effects, a hero that is all buffed, and a generic soundtrack that features chart topping songs. This film has none of that. This film is presented with no real special effects like explosions, features flawed characters, and a score that is just amazing to listen to. Then you have how Michel Hazanavicius (my word, that is a mouthful) unfolds the story by having everything told from the actors actually acting. There is no need for speaking and that is heavily embraced from start to finish. Now, I need to talk about the acting because it is astounding. Everyone from Jean Dujardin to Berenice Bejo to John Goodman to even a short cameo by Malcolm McDowell, this cast features, what I call, pure talent. The thing about these actors that separates them from any other cast of characters in 2012 is that they have to put all of the performance into their gestures, their movements. With talkies, you can express yourself with words and get the feelings across. Here they use their faces, arms, bodies in ways we have not see in a long while and what I see is more convincing acting then I have in most modern films. Even more shocking is one particular actor that, while small and scruffy, gives one of the most adorable and loyal of performances to date. In 2012 this film won best picture at the Academy Awards and rightfully so. This film is needed right now to remind us of why we watch films, why we pay ten dollars to go to the theater. This film is a true masterpiece and one I will not be surprised if I return to again and again. Note: this is the best film of 2012. Not my favorite. But it is in my top ten favorites.

The Artist is a silent film about the death of silent films.  It is arguably no better or worse than any number of silent pictures that were produced in the 1920s, with a narrative that rips-off Singing In the Rain just enough to matter.  As an attempt to replicate a long-defunct film style, it is I suppose a success.  It amuses and generally entertains, but it exists with little artistic style of its own.  It exists merely to be a rather standard silent film, and I would argue not even an exceptional one at that.  Like Hobo With a Shotgun and Super 8, The Artist is yet another example of the ongoing trend of genre exercise.  It offers no commentary on its era nor any particular insight into the nature of the silent picture.  Other than the fact that it is indeed a silent film made around 90 years after the rise of 'talkies', it has little to offer.  

The plot, in brief, concerns the professional and personal downfall of silent film star George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) when he is rendered irrelevant and unemployable after the rise of sound pictures.  His downward plunge is contrasted with young Peppy Miller (Bérénice Bejo) who begins her career with a chance encounter with the matinee idol and eventually rises to the top of the talking motion picture industry.  That's unfortunately pretty much it.  Like The Muppets and Hugo, it deals with artist who struggle to come to terms with their apparent artistic irrelevance.  But, without going into details, those films display a maturity and a somber acceptance of time that this picture does not.  This film plays more on the idea that once you're famous and/or successful in the entertainment industry, you have automatically earned the right to always be famous and a would-be comeback is your god-given right as a once-admired entertainer.  Moreover, unlike the two pictures noted above, there is nothing underneath the surface.  While Hugo is a plea for film preservation and The Muppets has an undercurrent of implicitly questioning the nostalgia that fueled its creation, The Artist is completely surface-level.      

The silent acting is relatively solid across the board, and the film earns kudos for not playing the relationship between the former idol and the rising movie star quite as you might expect.  Alas, it loses points for not giving Valentin's wife, played by Penelope Ann Miller, a single positive quality.  The rest of the cast (James Cromwell, John Goodman, Missi Pyle, Malcolm McDowell, etc.) exists purely as foils for the two leads.  It's disheartening to note that Valentin's dog gets more character development than anyone else in the supporting cast, as even he exists mainly to cause the audience to 'coo' on cue.  The film is simple in a fashion that silent films are often presumed of being, which makes the film almost an insult to the pioneering art form.

The Artist is a relatively entertaining gimmick, albeit one where it's primary gimmick is merely copying what was done without fanfare ninety-years ago.  It operates as an example of the 'things were better back in the day' without bothering to critique or even examine that concept.  Even Midnight In Paris, which I am not a fan of, had the decency to acknowledge the foolishness of trying to live in a theoretically better time (even if the lead character's obsession with the 1920s does cause him to 'improve' his life).  Outside of its implications as a cultural time capsule (our culture, natch), it is a trifle of a film, occasionally amusing and always gorgeous to look at.  But the film has no meaning, no real purpose except to tell a painfully simple story, and no real justification for 'just doing what they did back in the day'.  It is a copy of a prior art form, and it has no weight or relevance on its own.

From just about every technical standpoint, The Artist is a masterpiece; really it has to be, as it needs to hold the attention of a 21st century audience with the film making techniques of nearly a century ago and absent of any spoken dialogue or color. A great, consistently moving score help to keep you engaged with a plot that could easily lose you otherwise. Meticulous cinematography and art direction contribute as well. Michel Hazanavicius and his crew deserve tremendous credit for putting every aspect of a movie that might get glossed over because they're covered by strong acting under the microscope and making sure to get as close to perfection with them as they can. Even stuff I wouldn't normally notice like the snappy costumes stood out. And the performances are there to boot, as Jean Dujardin brims with the charm of a born leading man whose expressive physical work, comedic chops and ability to pour his heart into his face is remarkable. Berenice Bejo is a notch or two below Dujardin, but that doesn't mean she's not fantastic (she is). The supporting cast is wisely packed with actors not out of place in the setting who do so much storytelling with the way they move, particularly John Goodman, but also Missi Pyle and even James Cromwell; Penelope Ann Miller is a bit of a weak link, but she's not a particularly important cog. Finally the story being conveyed--the fall of a lovable but vain silent film star railing against talking pictures and his love story with the woman symbolizing his replacement--is strong with much to say. My big knock against The Artist would be its lack of staying power, meaning now that I've seen all the tricks (and there were some great ones, from everything I outlined to the gradual introduction of sound and so on), I really have no desire to watch it again. I'm also not sure how much my attention would have been held had I seen it in the theater as opposed to with my friends at their apartment, with us able to commentate over the whole thing (which we did). But hey, there are far worse things that being a darn near flawless piece of cinema that you only want to see once, and that dog was adorable.

Academy award winner Jean Dujardin is hilarious and heartbreaking in his actions of a largely popular silent film actor who's career begins to plummet at the birth of films with sound. Academy award nominee BÃ (C)rÃ (C)nice Bejo portrays the rising film actress who gets her break from his failure. She tries her best to help him from his forthcoming demise. The beautiful score, direction, and acting will keep you obsessed until the ending credits roll.

I just finished watching this movie and I really don't know where to begin with this review! It left me so pleasantly surprised and filled me up with sense of joy that all I want to do is watch it again! Don't miss watching this French romantic film directed by Michel Hazanavicius, and  starring Jean Dujardin and Bérénice Bejo. Everything in this movie is done the different way! It was filmed in only thirty-five days, made in the 1.33:1 screen ratio commonly used in the silent film era... and even that the movie was black and white it was shot in colour with a slightly lower frame rate of 22 fps as opposed to the standard 24 fps. The different way of doing things doesn't stop there: just check the casting choices and the resolution... or the amazing music composed by Ludovic Bource and recorded by Brussels Philharmonic and conducted by Ernst Van Tiel!

This well written, well calculated story which takes place in Hollywood between 1927 and 1932 focusing on the relationship of an older silent film star and a rising young actress is simply irresistible! I really don't care if Dujardin won the Best Actor Award at the 2011 Cannes, where the film premiered, or the six Golden Globe nominations with three wins, or twelve BAFTAs nominations with six wins or the ten Oscar nominations... this is a movie which will be remembered for the beauty of the cinematography itself!

I wish there were more of movies like this...

Is it possible to outright DISLIKE this film? (...I'm looking for no, you cretins). I can't imagine anyone having nothing good to say about it. It's far from original - not just because of its stylistical borrowing of movies past, but also its utterly conventional narrative - but if it doesn't completely charm your socks off, literally so they're on the floor in front of you, then I can say with confidence that someone has taken your soul. With its silents-vs-talkies story and Jean DuJardin's uncanny channelling of Gene Kelly, you could be forgiven for calling it a nostalgically modern rehash of Singin' In The Rain, one of the greatest movies ever made. But truthfully it is its own beast, and the relationship between silent hero George Valentin and new talkie sensation Peppy Miller is soppily, though believably, awesome. Berenice Bejo reminds me of Rachel McAdams, with her knowing but still somehow innocent elegance and electric smile, and DuJardin has unsurprisingly snaffled every award in the honeypot (as I write, the Oscars are in a few hours...) as the proud, tortured ex-megastar Valentin. Oh, and there's that dog and all.
Really beautiful movie, especially if you have always been delighted by the magic of movie making.

Few, if any leading male performers of 2011 were as haunting, earth-shattering and simply masterful as this French guy mugging for the camera because he can't talk. Hey, that's how everyone's making it sound, which is to be expected, considering the type of film Jean Dujardin is in. It's a black-and-white silent love letter to 1920s Hollywood and it came out in 2011; was there really any chance that the critics weren't going to love it? For all we know, it was supposed to be a talkie, but this French director-writer wanted to recreate good ol' American Hollywood so bad, yet could only afford other thickly-accented French people, so he had to keep the film silent because there was no way the stars were gonna pull off an American accent. Eh, maybe I'm reading too much into it, because if Michel Hazanavicius wanted these French people to go good ol' red-blooded 'Merican, he could have just given them an accent coach for about a week and they would come back speaking fluent redneck, because if you're from Europe, you seem to hold the secrets of the universe when it comes to accents. Well, it would seem that they didn't tell the score composer, Ludovic Bource, that secret, because although we haven't seen him actually try an American accent, after watching him try and power through speaking English, I think it's safe to say that he couldn't say, "Y'all" to save his life. Hey, I don't care if he starts speaking Klingon, just as long as the translation is, "I'm going to go compose some more music", because the guy knows his way around the tunes, yet not even the fabulous score can drown out the missteps that still boast in the midst of this silence.

This film is so hyper-active in its recreation of silent film that it's even adopting some of the flaws of a silent films. Yes, I said that 1920s silent films were flawed, because although there were limitations are the time, that didn't make the film any less flawed, and with this film actively adopting the spotty products of those limitations, it definately doesn't have an excuse. When they say that this film is silent, they weren't kidding, because outside of the score, there is little, if any audible atmosphere to really grip you, leaving the film to lapse in engagement so startlingly fast it's unreal. It doesn't help that, like the 1920s films that fancied audiences as little more than admirers of style rather than substance, this film rushes through its limited substance with very little depth, which isn't to say that this film doesn't dip its feet in some dramatic waters, though perhaps to deeply. Sure, there is still simplicity during the dramatic segment - so much so that the drama feels quite melodramatic -, but the transition is still so sudden and so contradictory to the preceding segments' energy that it further throws you out of the film. Now, I'm not saying that this silent film recreation experiment is a failure,  I'm saying that it succeeds too much to the point of lacking depth and consistency, due to the limitations it actively set up for itself. However, as problematic as this film's aspirations are, the project is undeniably ambitious, and through all of its flaws, the film lives up to the praisable ambitions much more than the problematic ones.

Going into this, it's hard not to see this film's intentions as gimmick, but when you look at the film, it's clearly not. They had to actually relearn the art of filmmaking to ensure the most heartfelt of homages, and sure enough, they nail it with no overemphasis on the style, leaving this highly unique visual concept to fit organically within the story, supplementing it to where the film feels complete with it. Well, Guillaume Schiffman's beautiful cinematography completes the film, as well as Ludovic Bource's riveting score that boasts the tone of the '20s, yet still has some subtle touches of contemporary score sensibilities, creating a composition that ices this cake and not only makes it more engaging than not, but sometimes creates some genuinely effective emotional resonance. The score certainly comes into play very nicely during the more energetic moments, such as dance sequences, all of which are pretty top-notch in and really add to the charm, something that the film still has more than enough of even without some of the flashier stuff, as Michel Hazanavicius manages to combine the simplistic charm of '20s films and the flashy charm of '20s people to create genuine charm that really wins you over for every brief moment where the film loses you. For this, we not only have thank the charm of the director, but also of his performers, all of whom are surprisingly lacking in stereotype and come out as very diverse, very human people of the time, with everyone fitting into this world seamlessly and charmingly with electric chemistry. Among this big batch of charmers stands out, well, Uggie the Dog, as well as the stunning (Even with those massive teeth) Bérénice Bejo, who manages to nail the excitement, as well as some of the changes that can be found when entering stardom with charm, as well authenticity that is complimented by her looking the part of a '20s young starlette to perfectly. The same can be said about Jean Dujardin, who couldn't possibly be more perfectly cast, because he's so 1920s cinema star that he looks less convincing with the Clark Gable-Stache, and as far as living up to the authenticity in his appearances, he nails it with crackling, explosive charisma emiting from him at almost all times, yet when the dramatic aspects come into play, he's graceful, maybe not to where he deserves major accolades, but enough so for you to see that this charmer may have more than just comedic talent in his blood.

Overall, the film gets to be ambitious to a fault, in that its silence and lack of depth leave many lulls in engagement, with the sudden and offputting tonal change at the halfway point exacerbating that disengagement, yet the film still makes up for its missteps by nailing the charm of both Hollywood and its products of the roaring '20s through beautiful cinematography, a fabulous score, lively production designs and plenty of electric charisma and between its colorful performers - particularly the gorgeous and very genuine Bérénice Bejo and the immensely charming Jean Dujardin... as well as the delightful Uggie the Dog -, ultimately leaving "The Artist" a thoroughly charming and consistently entertaining homage to the golden age of Hollywood.

The last time that a silent film has had such a profound impact on its audience was in 1928. It's now 2012 and "The Artist" has been enthralling audiences worldwide. Winner of the Academy Award for Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Actor, the film obviously had some awards to backup its credibility. To sum up the film in a sentence, I would say the movie is a silent film about the death of silent films. But lucky for you and me, (haha), I won't be summing this up in only a sentence. In fact, let me just say before I move on that I don't even know if anyone is reading this review. Flixter app on Facebook has changed so gerastically, that I don't believe its possible for anyone to see my reviews. So I guess I'm just writing reviews as a personal log for myself, and I guess thats fine. That way, I can always reference anything I've seen. Moving on. 

George Valentin is a silent film actor in 1927 and he's at the top of his game. He's the most famous and talked about actor in Hollywood. But as in most stories, fame doesn't last forever. Eventually, Hollywood incorporates sound into their productions, and Valentin fades away, while a woman that he helped get into the business, (whom he is in love with), becomes a famous actress. It's a story of envy and woe, but more so, its a tale of love. It's a generic, linear plot, and it needs to be, because the movie is completely silent, minus its soundtrack. 

The acting itself is absolutely fantastic, mainly because of one person; Jean Dujardin. He was absolutely phenomenal, from every aspect. He really gave a great performance, and this movie single handedly opened him up to American audiences, so I'm also pretty excited to see what movies come next from him. The whole brilliancy of his performance came in his physical characteristics, mostly from the face. He just had this physical tone that revealed all of his internal feelings. He was just really good. There are some other notable actors like Berenice Bejo, John Goodman, and James Cromwell, who were all pretty good. Great acting from start to finish. 

The cinematography was absolutely superb. This is the reason alone that made this movie feel like it was made in the 20's, and its aesthetic style transported me to a different time all together. The fact that the "cinematography" in "Hugo" one at the Oscars was preposterous. A film that was primarily CGI won. Thats ridiculous. Even so, this movie was wonderfully photographed. You know it, I know it, they know it...whatever. 

The soundtrack is great, and once again, it has to be because its our main sense of sound. Not sure who did the soundtrack but its pretty good. 

The movie really does have you captivated from its beginning. Its not that the movie itself does anything complicated or out of the ordinary to make you like it so much, but its just something that audiences deserve to see. Whether it be a movie to relate to in terms of economics, or maybe because you want to see something about love, it really does deliver. It takes everyone back to an era of great cinema, and its shot, like I said earlier, just like that. I think the movie serves as a reminder to Hollywood that they need to keep making good movies, not money makers. This movie is a gem and a tool. 

Michel Hazanavicius' impression on 1920's silent films was spot on, and lucky for us, we got a chance to experience it. The entire production itself is just something to marvel about. Its not a movie that brings us in with its power, or its brevity or whatever, but just its simplistic like-fullness. These kinds of movies can still entertain us, make us smile, and reel us in. Its up to my generation, to remember that.

"The Artist" is perfection.  There is not a scene that could find a better angle, a facial expression that could be more vivid, or a musical moment that could be more emotional.  A silent film about the end of the Silent Film Era.  Genius.  The heart of this film is the Oscar-winning musical score written by Ludovic Bource, paying tribute to many film scores over the years while creating a perfect emotional atmosphere (whether it is anger or love) in which the actors can grow without the aid of dialogue.  The score matches the stereotype of silent film music while being fresh, original, and simply heartwrenching at times (particularly the "Vertigo" segment).  Not only is the music incredibly effective, but so is the strategic use of complete silence, creating its own beautiful soundtrack of frustration and contemplation.  The scene with the sound effects was very cool and perfectly supported the storyline of the film.  One of my favorite visuals is the orchestral conductor in the front of the movie house conducting the pit with the film on the big screen behind him.  People from my generation (and a few generations beforehand) never had the opportunity to experience silent films in the theater.  But not only does this film give perspective into this entirely different world, it creates an authentic experience by presenting this film within a film as it wouldâ(TM)ve been viewed in the 20â(TM)s.  This film won 5 Oscars but easily could have won in all 10 of its nominated categories.  The visuals are so wonderful, incorporating many of the traditional plot devices that you expect to find in a silent film with the refined visual style of today's films.  It seems that the majority of films from the silent era had simple stories that could easily be told without dialogue, but "The Artist" provides vivid character development throughout its complex plot.  How does it work?  Virtuosic acting.  Dialogue is not needed when the faces of these actors tell every emotion and thought.  Jean Dujardin's smile is out of this world - if you didn't know that this film is ficticious, you would assume that George Valentin truly was an actor from the Silent Film Era.  The look of love on his face, his interactions with "The Dog," and his frustrated expressions all give him a very authentic look.  It is no surprise that he won the Oscar for Best Actor.  I was actually quite sad that Berenice Bejo did not receive an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.  She was absolutely charming, from her audition as an extra to her final dance with Valentin - who could resist that smile (and beauty mark)?  John Goodman and James Cromwell were also perfectly cast in their roles.  This film is pure magic.  Typically the dialogue of a film is what stirs my emotions, but this film somehow made me cry my eyes out without a single word, creating one of the most overwhelming and beautiful moments in any film - no need for fancy cinematography or a romantic line.  Simply, a driver entering a car after an auction and a woman visiting the love of her life in a hospital.  And after experiencing every emotion in the book from this simple film, you will lean back and your chair and simply say "Wow."  Once in a generation, there is a film transcends all others.  This is "The Artist."

I suppose it's called poetic justice when a silent film can leave one speechless, but that is exactly the artistic achievement of Michael Hazanavicius', 'The Artist'. An homage that wears it's influences on it's sleeve, this 21st century silent picture is a tribute to why we fell in love with cinema in the first place.

The film stars Jean Dujardin as George Valentin, a 1920's silent movie star at the precipice of his popularity. He is suave, charismatic, and, most importantly, has a well trimmed mustache. John Goodman plays his producer, James Cromwell his personal chauffer, and Uggie the dog plays his personal metaphor (what's that saying about dogs and tricks?). While working on one of his new films, George unwittingly launches the career of Peppy Miller (Bérénice Bejo), a bubbly, energetic extra with hopes of being a star herself. 

By the late 20's, the film studios begin introducing sound. From the start, George adamantly refuses to adapt to the industry's new filmmaking formula, proclaiming himself to be "an artist" that people come to see, not hear. As his star begins to fade, Peppy's only gets brighter, becoming Hollywood's newest darling starlet of the talkies. After his own failed filmmaking endeavors, made worse by the 1929 stock market crash, George loses his means and meaning in life. As he struggles with his sudden destitution, Peppy resolves to help the man that she adores, admires, loves and owes her entire existence to. 

Many people would compare 'The Artist' to films like 'Singin' in The Rain' and 'Sunset Boulevard', and they would have good reason to. But this film is more like 2010's 'The Illusionist', an animated film about a stage magician who is unable to cope with the death of his beloved vaudeville and the birth of rock n roll. On the surface, George appears to be a stubborn, uncompromising man who rejects change based on the principle of rejecting it. But as the film carries on, we soon realize that like the illusionist, this artist is not unwilling, but simply unable to change, which makes his downfall even more tragic. It is not that he hates rock n roll, it's that he can't play the instruments.

But that's not where the film referencing stops. Along with themes from 'Singin' in The Rain' and 'Sunset Boulevard' (and a similar dance sequence from the former), Hazanavicius fills his movie with aspects of classic films that have no doubt inspired him. For instance, there is a breakfast table montage scene that closely resembles that of Orson Welles' 'Citizen Kane' and a segment of the score comes directly from Alfred Hitchcock's 'Vertigo'. It is important to understand, however, that this is a far cry from mere plagiarism. Hazanavicius utilizes these aspects as a literal metaphor for how this film could not have been made without the inspiration and influences that these classics have engendered. 'The Artist' is not daringly original, and it does not pretend to be. In fact, that's the point. Hazanavicius does not try to pass off these scenes as his own; he assumes that you know them before hand and that you will readily recognize them. He and his film are proudly esoteric, and it never panders or condescends to the audience.  

But what about the general audience, you may ask. Well, as a French, black and white, silent film, what do you think? In this rare case, forget the general audience. This film is a love letter, and love letters are not written for everybody to read. Love letters are to be received by people who share the same passion and adoration for the subject matter as the auteur himself, and it's quite evident that Hazanavicius intends his film to be embraced by people who love classical Hollywood as much as he does; general audience be damned. This film is endlessly charming, it's characters endlessly endearing, and it's story endlessly ubiquitous. If you love the pictures, you'll love this one too.
