With every technical advance-in this case, the addition of sound to film in the early 30s-we lose something. Sure, we shake off much of the cheesy hamming that made Vaudevillians such great silent screen actors. However, we also lose the beautiful subtlety of expression and the experiments in cinematography.

As Gloria Swanson famously said in Sunset Boulevard, "We didn't need dialogue. We had faces!"

The Artist is a silent, black and white flick that takes us on a nifty journey of nostalgia.

Dujardin is a silent film actor, in the style of Valentino with a little Errol Flynn rakishness thrown in. When one of his adoring fans, Bejo, accidentally bumps into him, she finds herself on the way to Hollywoodland stardom. She becomes famous in talkies, just as his star fades-again, like Valentino. He self-destructs and only her secret love and care protects him. Well, that and the loyalty of his awesome dog!

It's a pretty simple story, but silent films always were. Camera shots and background sets basically pound the themes home in a fun way. The score prevails, but small experiments in sound effects give us a sense of what we gave up with the introduction of noise. The Artist teaches us the power of faces and body language.

The idea could've been gimmicky, but a deep respect for silent films makes this flick a joy to behold.

"Out with the old, in with the new".  It's what they said about silent films when the advent of "talkies" proved to be more than just a passing fad.  It's what they said about many of those silent age actors too, who didn't have a voice for film, and who were soon replaced by other faces and names.  Of course new isn't necessarily always better.  At least that's what George Valentin (Jean Dujardin in an academy award winning performance) would say.  When shown a film clip of a talkie for the first time, he scoffs at it's ridiculousness: where is the artistry?  Valentin is an enormously successful silent film star who has just about the whole world wrapped around his finger, he's charismatic, dashing, without guile; his star power radiates like a super nova.  Leaving one of his sold out movie premieres, he bumps into a young woman by the name of Peppy Miller (BÃ (C)rÃ (C)nice Bejo), who takes an ackward situation and turns it into a paparazzi moment, schmoozing for the cameras.  It's all Valentin can do to keep up with her.  "Who's That Girl?" reads the Variety page headlines.  Peppy takes a copy with her to a movie audition, determined to make sure the producers know.  Of course Valentin runs into her again, as fate must seemingly decree, and he insists she try out for a part in his movie.  

The rise of one star and the fall of another has been done many times in hollywood, A Star is Born, All About Eve, Singin' in the Rain (even some of those Busby Berkeley musicals) have all shared similar themes, but The Artist is only marginally about that.  How about the actual artist himself?  The man who decrees he'd rather fail by his own creation than succeed pandering to some imagined audience.  Artists of the silent screen like Buster Keaton or Douglas Fairbanks (who bears more than a passing resemblance to Dujardin's Valentin character, in both appearance and mannerisms) saw their creativity shackled as sound became the standard and their unique gifts were constrained to studio pigeon holes.  In "The Artist", Valentin makes a film of unique beauty, financed by his own money, and ignored by a public still reeling from the stock market crash of 1929.  His failure is not from lack of anything, save timing.  But The Artist is only marginally about that too.  To get to the heart of the matter, The Artist is really and simply about love.  Pride makes it difficult to surrender sometimes.  Sometimes we'd rather die than admit defeat at an erroneous cause.  But what about the man who doesn't surrender to love?  The man who is too afraid to let someone see the "real" him?  More than anything, Valentin spends the movie running away from love and the surrender he must give to it.

It's no surprise "The Artist" won five oscars (Best Costume Design, Best Directing, Best Original Score, Best Lead Actor, and Best Film of the Year), it's production is nearly flawless from one end to the other.  Lead actor Jean Dujardin is positively mesmerizing as Valentin and does what few contemporary actors could achieve, his movements on the screen are like that of a ballet dancer's.  The director, Michel Hazanavicius, crafts a painstakingly accurate tribute to films not just of the silent era but of the golden age of film in general.  With black and white, it's all shadows and light for cinematographers, with Hazanavicius, it's all about the staircase (so many scenes revolve around staircases in this movie, watch and see if you don't notice this).  It's the kind of film that will continue to stand out in one's memory years after seeing it, I'm sure.  Above all, it's sweetly old-fashioned and poignant, something very rare for a film these days.  Simply put, it's beautiful.

I know of only one real try at making a silent movie since the genre died of natural death in the thirties; that was the Mel Brooks 1976 parody 'Silent Movie'. I did not go to see that film and don't plan to. While technically not a real silent movie, 'The Artist' is as close as you'll ever come to it; it has an actual soundtrack which is almost exclusively music with very few sound effects and, like Brooks' film, only one word is spoken, hence, it can't be called a silent movie.

If it had not fared so well at all my usual sources and all the unusual ones as well, I doubt I would have bothered watching it; heyâ¦ it's a silent movie. While I've seen most all the 2011 movies that were nominated for best picture and written reviews of them, only 'The Artist" I can say truly is a bold and daring artistic production. I've read countless reviews of this movie and though other nominees were worthy of the prize, such madness deserved to win. It not only was mad to attempt it, it overlapped into genius because it was done successfully. There are no flaws in this production; it pays homage to silent movies by being just that, flawless. It has a beautiful story, the actors are compelling and it calls to sentiments any modern movie could boast of conveying.

For history buffs: The silent movies, in the early thirties, were the sole source of happy escape from the hard times (the great depression) of that period. Anyone going through hard times now deserves to see this movie; thankfully, you need not be French or American to enjoy it.

Other reviewers have at length outlined the storyline, well summarized on this site, so you don't need to read it again from me; it was brilliant to make that particular story in silent form. I could go on about the wonderful musical score, without which it could not have worked so well; the directing by Michel Hazanavicius, who wrote the script and poured all he had to give toward making it a well done movie, deserves all the rewards he has received, including public admiration from his gorgeous wife, the co-star of the movie. I liked the whole cast, no exceptions. Did I like the movie? I loved it.

*George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) is the biggest star in Hollywood who along with his companion, the dog Jack appears in countless box office successes. His influence among the directors and producers in Hollywood, is huge and he gives a cute unknown female extra a start, when he convinces a director to cast her. The girl's name is Peppy Miller (Benerice Bejo) and a few years later, she'd become the biggest name on the screen. George Valentine, does sadly belong to the handfull of actors that wouldn't make the transition to sound movies and almost from one day to another he goes from being the biggest star in Hollywood, till forgotten and ruined. Peppy, on the other hand, never forgets the kindness George showed her and is aware of that it's because of him that she broke through. She tries hard to help him now when he's down and out.* 

Among the cast, you'll spot John Goodman as the Hollywood-director and Malcolm McDowell as George's butler.

Had looked forward to see this movie for so long, I was almost a little bit nervous when I was about to watch it. I don't know if it fully lived up to my expectations (after hearing and reading about all it's praise and oscar winnings). You have to keep in mind that I have watched several hundreds of silent movies from the period 1900-1930, and can easily notice if there are any details that makes it look less authenthic. I don't want you to believe that I was looking for "mistakes" and so on, it's just that some things are pretty obvious if you've seen a few silent flicks before (which I'm sure many people have).
What bothered me, was that the character "Peppy Miller" made quite extreme gestures that you did rarely see in movies from 1927 (which I think the year was supposed to be). It was common many years before, but the acting was pretty much toned down towards the end of the 1920s, and the acting in silent movies didn't look like that at all. The developement in movie acting had gone further and looked less theatrical and more "movie-like" by then.
I am lenient towards the fact that Peppy didn't at all look like any of the other starlets from that time. The beauty ideal was different then, and women were supposed to have subtle features, not at all like today. But since there were exceptions even then, (look at Gloria Swanson for example, I think I shouldn't be to hard on the film makers). 
The main character on the other hand; George Valentin, really corresponded to the acting and the popular looks of actors from that time. You could easily tell that he has been studying Douglas Fairbanks acting a whole lot, which I don't think is any secret.

I really like the scene when a seemingly unknown extra is practising tap dancing, with a screen covering her upper body and face, and George Valentine is "duelling" her. It turned out that the extra was the soon to be famous Peppy Miller (who many years later would become George's dancing partner on screen!).
But my favorite scene must be when George is dreaming a nightmare, as a bad omen, about everybody being able to speak but him, just before the sound era had struck.

So all in all, I'm giving this movie a solid 80% which means that I really liked it. I thought it was an unusually innovative, creative and playfull movie, flirting a lot with the past (and though I was not 100% charmed, I know that many others were). It had some very sweet and nostalgic elements, for example the relationship between George and Peppy, which was non-sexual. Those kind of relationships was not as unusual in movies from that time as it is today, and it respresented some old victorian ideals which were still shown in movies then, even though the 1920s were known as a decadent and free spirit decade.

The artist tells a story about a successful film  actor who slowly falls in his career regarding changes to modern sound technology. The movie is very amusing and enjoyable to watch. Well worth all its awards. 
Unfortunately, a journalist for the sun news paper heavily criticized the film while trying the manipulate the British public in disliking the film. He quoted that The Artist does not deserve its awards for two main reasons. One because it's a silent black and white movie, and two because the film was French. If you are a reader of the sun, please do not be influenced by its criticisms. I don't quite think that the sun fully understood the context of The Artist, and what is was trying to present. 
In my opinion, I think the movie also tells a story which relates to how modern technology effects art. As we can see in the film, audio technology changed movies bringing forward a new revolution in film making. Although this was a positive development, silent films still held a witty and amusing style which has now been forgotten and left behind forever. Today we are also experiencing a new revolution as it appears that the future of movies may be all in 3D. But is this what art should be about? Should technology tack over? Should our expectations in movies change because of technical developments? Should we forget about the past film making styles. Please note that this is just my opinion. None of my material has been researched, but I personally think that the movie is presenting a revolution which happened in the past so we can understand changes for the future.
If I am correct, then I guess that this is where the films holds its finest quality. It shows us that technology does benefit movies, but we still shouldn't forget about the past as art does not have to be bound to modern technology. The fact that the film is in silent black and white demonstrates my opinion because the movie follows an old style which still entertains the modern viewer. Our new revolution in 3D cinema can now question us in a modern point of view. Will 3D cinema now take away old qualities in story telling like how audio changed films in the past?
I believe that the sun didn't understand what the film was trying to present as they believed  The Artist  only won awards because it followed an old style of film making which stood out from the rest of the films. They even pointed out that the film couldn't be any good because it was French? This does confuse me because there are many good French film makers such as Jean-Pierre Jeunet, and Luc Besson for example. I had extreme apprehension seeing The Artist. It's not because of the fact that it's a silent movie or that it's in black and white. Those kinds of things, I welcome. Frankly, I hesitated because of the idea that someone made a silent movie. It won best picture this past year and I thought that maybe it was just a load of douchebaggery. After all, if you want to suck off Hollywood, make a movie about movies. That wasn't the case. Well, maybe the last part, but certainly not the first.

See, we stopped making silent movies because technology changed. It wasn't because the artistry changed or anything of the sort. Times changed and it was time to adapt. There were, however, a number of actors and filmmakers that did not welcome this change. Even Charlie Chaplin was against it. They thought that it was a fad and that it would go away. And it didn't.

The Artist, starring an incredible Jean Dujardin, tells exactly that story. We have a man gripping onto his livelihood while making silent movies.

One of the most memorable things about this movie, aside from the fact that it was silent, was the direction of photography. It's in this formalist vein, but doesn't draw attention to itself too much. It truly is beautiful to look at. Each shot is composed very carefully giving the viewer the best possible shot each scene.

Everyone involved gave a wonderful performance. Everyone from John Goodman, James Cromwell, and the all-too-briefly-seen Malcolm McDowell. Bérénice Bejo, our secondary lead, did a terrific job as Peppy Miller, a carefree rising star. Each actor gave a performance that was believable without having to use a lot of words. They were all expressive enough to give you all of the clues as to how they are feeling without looking like flapping chickens.

The fact of the matter is this movie is a niche movie. It's not something that will break records at the box office or draw even a remotely full crowd in middle-America. It's a movie that movie-lovers go to see. It's the kind of movie that people call a "film."

It's funny how within the same year we had Hugo, a Hollywood film that glorified the early French cinema, and The Artist, a French film that glorified the early Hollywood cinema. Yet both are very different as independent movies. Perhaps these two films shouldn't be compared like this, but I can't help it. To me Hugo feels more familiar. It tried to portray how movies were made during that time, but it still feels much more recent, the films aesthetics play to the norms of the modern day. All the colours, all the visuals. The setting is historical, but it's still a film that has clearly been done during the 21th century.

Not so much with The Artist, which genuinely feels and looks like a silent film of the early 20th century. And I love it because of it. The 1.33:1 screen ratio, the complete lack of dialogue or even environmental sounds (with one very haunting and effective exception), the use of music to tell a story, the constant mugging that still manages to look somewhat genuine, the black-and-white visuals - they all feel real and only the quality of the picture separates this from a genuine silent film. Well, that, and some singular scenes where the movie actually has some sound effects to create certain effects. Which is a point to the movie's favour, mind you, because even though this movie tries to imitate a silent film as much as possible, it still recognizes the fact that it's a modern film and can use certain effects that were not available during the time of its role models. Furthermore, the subject of the film is the coming of the so called talkies, so the occasional use of sound is easily called for.

So it really is a rather good film. Its very idea is easily the best part of it, but the individual aspects of the film easily keep up. The actors are very talented at what they do with Jean Dujardin's performance being every bit Oscar-worthy, though I personally think that Bérénice Bejo does equally good job as his counterpart. There's just this genuine joy to her and her dancing. And of course the music is fantastic. It has to be or the film just wouldn't work, because the score is the only thing that we will hear most of the time.

The movie has no obvious flaws, though the story is both intriguing and a bit predictable at the same time. But that's me nitpicking. It's a good movie and easily worth your time. And most importantly: it made me interested in silent films. And to this film that is the highest compliment that anyone can assign.

The critically acclaimed winner of so many Academy Awards, The Artist sounded like a beautiful spectacle.
 
Frankly, it was. The Artist is the first feature length silent film I have ever seen, and it really gave me an effective sense of what the industry was all about during the 1920's era. The narrative cleverly combines the tales of actors John Gilbert and Douglas Fairbanks into an amalgamated character, George Valentin. He is a very sympathetic character who captures our love without ever having to speak to do so, and the way that the story revolves around him through his success and his failure is brilliant. The tale is very reminiscent of the 1937 film A Star is Born and the 1954 remake. In that sense, it is rather predictable at times. And yet, at the same time it remains a beautiful homage to the spectacular era where cinema triumphed so graciously. The Artist does not have the most groundbreaking story, but it capitalises on a demand for nostalgia which has taken cinema by storm in recent years and takes them back to a time in cinematic history through examining a narrative which relates to the time period and exploring it with an ideal style to convey that. There is no denying the stylish charm of The Artist which is put into play by the Academy Award winning work of director Michel Hazanavicius. His eye for imagery and passion for making an amazing film really makes him the titular artist, and his work is truly a masterpiece of contemporary filmmaking.
From a technical perspective, there is nothing to complain about with The Artist. Presented in a 3:4 aspect ratio with cinematography which cleverly manipulates the lighting and uses various techniques to present narrative symbolism, while maintaining enough classical techiques to mirror the style of its intended time frame. It is a beautiful film for how it captures the wonderful costumes and scenery all in black and white, as well as the production design which has some subtle yet clever moments which make use of proscenium. The visual experience of The Artist is enough to warrant its viewing, but it is made even better by the music in the film. 
Being a silent film, The Artist relies on physical acting and a proper musical score to set the mood, and it does that perfectly. 
The musical score in The Artist is extremely important. Due to being a silent film, the music is one of the key things driving the narrative is the music. The musical score for The Artist is absolutely beautiful. It is perfectly atmospheric, nailing the moods of the more intense scenes as well as the lighthearted ones. The musical score in The Artist is beautiful because even though the film does not have to rely on it too much as a narrative device, it is always there to help keep things moving along the track and it is beautiful to embrace. Frankly, The Artist is a treat on the ears nearly as much as the eyes. I say nearly because the visual experience of the film is given an extra push by the cast who all subscribe to the expressionist nature of the film and give powerful performances.
We live in a world dominated by talking film characters, and yet Jean Dujardin's magnificent leading performance in The Artist reminds us just how much an actor can carry a film with solely physical acting. Jean Dujardin's performance as George Valentin is a revalation because his facial expressions are always so clear in expressing his emotional status while his physical movements are always in tone with how he feels, and yet at the same time he is also such a charmingly handsome man that he is always a treat to look at. Jean Dujardin is a handsome actor and a thoroughly talented one who doesn't have to speak to make this clear to viewers as he captures the development of George Valentin through his success, his relationships, his career downfall and his descent into depression without even the briefest falter. His performance is remarkable because he single handily goes to show just how many emotions can be expressed solely through the art of a physical performance, and through doing so he easily establishes himself in the role of a talented silent movie actor by being one for the film. His leading performance is remarkable and easily Academy Award calibre.
Bernice Bejo is also wonderful. Though she never speaks for the entire film, her beautiful smile, sense of innocence and artificial beauty spot make her reminiscent of Marilyn Monroe while her passionate spirit and dedication to the role evoke memories of Judy Garland. She combines the spirit of the two legendary actresses and expresses it solely through as physical demeanour in The Artist, and there could not have been a more perfect woman to cast in the role of Peppy Miller. Bernice Bejo really does a good job because of how she remains a likable character the entire time, always there to support George Valentin and never losing sight of her love of him even through all her success. The way that Bernice Bejo interacts with Jean Dujardin is wonderful just because of how much emotion comes from the two actors facing each other and embracing their respective talents, so they are the perfect duo to be leading The Artist. Even though Jean Dujardin is unbeatable, Bernice Bejo holds her own whenever on screen which makes her essential whenever she is around and always a likable foil.
Also, there is no denying the importance of Uggie. Being the canine actor trained to perform all kinds of tricks, Uggie's performance in The Artist is one of the finest performances ever given by an animal on film. He manages to actually show all kinds of emotions, interact with the universe of the film as best as possible and still remain such a cute character. Uggie's talents are beyond what so many would expect from a dog, so he is a screen stealer whenever he is around. Uggie is an incredibly well trained actor, and his performance in The Artist is the finest I have ever seen a Canine deliver.
John Goodman's supporting role is also strong.

So though The Artist has a familiar plot device, it is an incredible experience for the eyes and the ears thanks to Michel Hazanavicius' magnificent directorial work, Ludovic Bource's powerful musical score and the flawless performances from Jean Dujardin, Bernice Bejo and Uggie.

I have fallen in love with Cinema all over again.

 

Back in the Golden Age of film-making, most movies were silent and relied on actors who could do big, theatrical performances and a bit of camera mugging to convey emotions to the audience. It was a simpler time in which we didn't have special effects or CGI to wow the crowds. Film-makers simply needed a good story, and a good actor, the rest would follow.

 

One man, Michel Hazanavicius, is obviously a fan of this era and has graced the world of cinema with "The Artist". A film which is a throwback to the good ol' days of the Motion Picture Industry when silence was king and talkies were just around the corner. See, rather than make a conventional movie, i.e. anything that is produced by Michael Bay, stars Tom Cruise, is adapted from a comic book or has fake vampires; this man has put real thought and effort into his latest work which is a tribute to the films of the yesteryear.

 

I love this film.

 

I do.

 

Really.

 

This goes on my top ten list.

 

Now, as I mentioned in a previous review, my peers of my generation turned their noses up at a film like this.

 

"Black and white?" They said. "Black and white film? SILENT?"

 

They looked at me agog.

 

"How can you like a film like that?"

 

Well, off the top of my head:

 

1) Cinema and films in general are a Visual art. You force your eyes to stare at the screen and your brain interprets what it sees into information for you to understand. Sure, dialogue and sound effects are nice, but these are not compulsory ingredients. Imagine your smart phone with all its apps. Sure, the apps are a sweet little accessory that help you take pleasure in using your phone, but at the end of the day it's still a phone and you use it for its most basic function. (I'm not talking about texting.)

2) People seem to forget that if it were not for the pioneers of film-making in the 20's and 30's such as Chaplin, Keaton, Lloyd, Capra, Hitchcock, Hawks and even the people responsible for German expressionism; we would not have the cinema you and I know today. Surely we should remember what these people achieved, despite poor technology, low budgets and small star power. Surely we should watch their films and think "These films stand the test of time, these films made me think, these films have influenced directors of today!" instead of "Black and white? Boooooooooooring!"

3) Black and white films are gorgeous to look at. The fact that film-makers of that time had to consider the lighting and contrast of each shot before the cameras started rolling is brilliant. Trying to figure out what the overall look of your masterpiece should be, as opposed to "Has Mr Cruise been given his Cappuccino?", definitely sets you apart from other film-makers. One of my favourite scenes from "It's a Wonderful Life" is when George Bailey (whilst in the world he was not born in) visits his house, now derelict and filled with cobwebs. As his face gets closer and closer to the camera it becomes enveloped in shadow. There's NO dialogue. None is required. The darkness symbolises isolation, the man slowly fading away from reality, cut off from all that he knows, and there's no one to guide him home. Only that could have been achieved in black and white. And it is gorgeous.

 

But I digress...

 

"The Artist" tells the story of an actor who is at the top of his game during the silent era. He discovers a young girl who wants to be an actress, sets her on the right path, then watches in despair as she begins to make "talkies". Realising that audiences no longer want to watch the man who says nothing, can he recoup his losses?

 

For a film with no dialogue, the acting is astounding from an all star cast. Every emotion is conveyed perfectly from the over dramatic scream, to a simple raising of an eyebrow. It's all there. It just goes to show you that actors can do their job, even when given little material to work with.

 

However, what really pleases a film buff like me though is the attention to detail. The late 20's are meticulously recreated. I'm not talking about props or costumes though. The film itself (and its films within the film) has been shot as it would have been from that period of time. There are long, focused shots on people speaking, to give audiences a chance to read lips before the title card is flagged on-screen, the sets have that made-on-the-cheap feel, there's even that dodgy bluescreen background they used to use when a character drives around in their car. And it's all filmed in a nostalgia inducing 4:3 ratio.

 

Whilst sitting in the cinema, two girls were in the row behind me. From the sound of it, one had dragged her best friend along to see the film because it was different. (Good for you sweetheart!) The friend was complaining that she wanted to see "War-Horse", despite reassurance from the girl that this feature film would be better.

 

"Besides, there's a wee dug in it!" The girl said to her friend.

"Ok," she replied. But added sulkily: "It better be, I'm not paying £6 to see some old sh**e."

 

Ah, the youth of today. So stupid, yet they get all the discounts!

 

As the opening credits appeared on screen I sat nervously anticipating to hear the girls give out a banshee wail of horror, realising what they had let themselves in for. Culture!

 

To my surprise though, they were silent. Fixated on what they saw. I looked around and could just make out that everyone else in the cinema was also engrossed. It was so quiet... Like they were in a museum, and had stumbled upon an ancient relic, pondering at what its purpose could possibly be.

 

As the end credits rolled, I had a huge grin on my face. I'm not sure if it was the movie, or the round of applause it was receiving.

 

Words cannot do this film justice. This is an affectionate, tender tribute to the men and women who paved the way for today's generation of entertainers, and solidly confirms that the silent era never really died. It just went away for a while. Whatever this film is nominated for at the Academy, it deserves! Screenwriter William Goldman once said that no-one really knows what the next big thing will be, until you see Hollywood trying to replicate its success. In 2008 we had "The Dark Knight" and films became darker in tone. In 2009/10 we had "Avatar", and with it we saw jumps in realistic CGI effects.

 

This year we have "The Artist", and I wouldn't be surprised if we saw another "Non-talkie" any time soon...

"The Artist," is full of silent but over-praised charm 

	As some of you may be aware, last weekend the nominations for this year's Academy Awards were announced. Most were expected, some were surprises and there were more than few snubs, but all of that can be covered later. 
The most important issue is, despite my best efforts, there are still three Best Picture nominated films I haven't seen as of yet, so starting this week I'm going to focus on getting those done. First up is probably the film with the most buzz and has been, until recently, highly elusive. 
The film is titled "The Artist" and reason for its high profile status boils down to the fact that it's a silent movie. You heard me right; this is a classic, early 20th century style silent movie, with the constant score and dialogue cards and everything. And while certainly modern elements find their way into the picture, for the most part this is the most classic of films, in both execution and content.
	Even without dialogue, the narrative of "The Artist" is quite apparent. George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) is a silent film star working for the fictional Kinograph studios. After the successful debut of his most recent film, Valentin is participating in a photo shoot when a young woman, Peppy Miller (Bérénice Bejo), bumps into him. Used to making a show for the cameras, Valentin plays it up and soon Peppy finds herself on the front page of local newspapers. She's inspired to try out for work as an actress, which Valentin helps her break into.
	However, as Peppy's star begins to rise in Hollywood, Valentin's world is turned upside-down with the sudden popularity boom of talkies, films with sound. Valentin is soon faced with the reality that the film world might just move on without him.
	As I mentioned before, the big story with this film is that it's a silent movie...about the decline of silent movies. And while I certainly appreciate the inherent cleverness of that idea, it's the overall execution that sells the film. Great care was taken to try and capture the spirit of classic Hollywood. Without dialogue, of course, it's all on the actor's ability to actually act; that, and a constant, expressive and highly adaptive score from Ludovic Bource.
	Now here's where this review starts to get murky. While I certainly appreciate the effort taken to make this film, the idea, the aesthetic and the sense of powerful nostalgia put into this piece.  I cannot help but compare it to the rest of 2011's best; especially with the grand accolades the cinematic world is bestowing on this saying this film.
	The simple fact of the matter is, in terms of actual content, this film lacks depth. It's all about the atmosphere and experience. The characters and the story? They're, for lack of a better word, kind of shallow. This is hardly the first film to tell the story of the downfall of silent movies. "Sunset Boulevard" comes to mind, amongst various others. Just because dialogue isn't being used to tell the story doesn't mean the message is any more original.
	The thing is, there's a reason films did transition to using sound, because the addition of dialogue adds so many layers of complexity to a film, its story and its characters. I think of a film like "The Descendants" and the amazing gamut of emotions it presents, or "The Ides of March" which wasn't even nominated, and "The Artist" couldn't hope to compete with them in terms of depth. The truth is, when you strip away the nostalgia and the pretty paint, making "The Artist" a silent movie is basically a gimmick.
	If you were to add dialogue to this piece, it would be completely unremarkable. And of course, almost everyone would protest that "the lack of dialogue is the whole point," to which I would respond that if the fact that your movie has no sound is the entire point, then it's not a complete movie. Best Picture is about more than being "interesting" or "classic." It's about exemplifying the best of what this entire entertainment medium has to offer, and truth is the story and characters of "The Artist," which to me are critical parts of that medium, are rather simple, and you can't be Best Picture if you have anything "simple" in your movie.
	This is not intended as an attack on "The Artist." I thought the film was quite entertaining, and a wonderful artistic achievement. It deserves awards for the amazing work people did to make it come to life. But it's not "Best Picture," Jean Dujardin is not best actor, and Michel Hazanavicius certainly didn't write the best screenplay. This film is indeed an impressive work of art, but I think the Academy and the press have become a bit too enamored with nostalgia of late. This is a vote for what is best now, not a vote for what you thought the golden age of cinema was.
Grade: B+

In this silent, black and white movie, George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) is a huge silent film actor living in the late 20s. As his career reaches a high-point, young up-and-comer Peppy Miller (Berenice Bejo) befriends this veteran actor. Soon afterwards, however, silent films give way to talkies, which Valentin despises. Then the dirty thirties come rolling in and George ends up bankrupt.

For three years in a row now, the Academy Award for Best Picture has gone to the wrong movie. Not necessarily a bad movie, but the wrong movie. In 2009, it went to the war-time drama directed by James Cameron's ex, The Hurt Locker, which should've easily been won by films like Up, or Inglorious Basterds. The following year, The King's Speech, about King George VI's struggle with his impediment. A great film, but an award that should've gone to Social Network, or 127 Hours or even Toy Story 3.

And then we come to The Artist. A good film, but not the absolute best and definitely not as fabulous as everyone anticipated it to be.

I'm not a hypocrite, nor do I hate the classic films of yar. In fact, I think a lot of silent/black and white movies are great. But there's a reason why the world doesn't make silent films anymore. They're a little dull. I mean, if they never made color films, then movies like Avatar or Toy Story 3 or other very colorful movies would be absolutely redundant, and drain out the magic. And because of people's attention spans and impatience, speaking is almost essential in modern-day films.

But what Michel Hazanavicius has done is magical in itself. He managed to take a story, which could've been totally doable in color and talking, but he took a massive gamble in making making this kind of a movie. Did it pay off? Yes and no. Yes because it's so refreshing in making a movie showing actors using funny slapstick-y humour rather than saying a funny line of dialogue and relying on their facial expressions as well. And no because some people may have the impression that people have moved on from this.

Jean Dujardin plays a very likeable protagonist in George Valentin. This foreign actor whom I've never seen a movie with him in it before, but he is a fantastic actor. And he really gives Valentin a charm and swagger and suave that makes you really like this guy, which is different from other films of today who have a complete jerk as the protagonist. His romantic interest Peppy Miller, played by Berenice Bejo, is also likeable enough and pretty enough to win people over as well. The only bad thing about the acting is that I wish John Goodman had more scenes in the movie, because John Goodman is awesome!

On the technical side of things, the artisans on The Artist do a fair job. Including the costume designer Mark Bridges (who mind you won an Oscar), the production designers, composer Ludovic Bource (who also won that prestigious award) and sound editing. I'm not kidding, there is sound in this movie. I'm not hinting where, but when it does appear it's totally overwhelming.

Good acting, good writing/directing, a risky premise, but a simple and doable storyline, The Artist is somewhat overrated, and won't appeal to everyone, but certain film nuts will go bananas for the movie that proves silence is golden.

*** out of ****
FINAL VERDICT: 77%

A worthy Oscar-winner, but not the best of 2011. Either way, it's still visually pleasing, artistically filmed, and full of classic charm. 

PLOT:George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) is the Hollywood-hit silent film star in the late 1920s. Everybody loves him and he is rich with a wife and a dog which appears in the pictures with him. One day after the premiere of one of his films, he "runs into" a young lady named Peppy Miller (Berenice Bejo) and immediately starts to joke with her. During the filming of another of his works, he finds Peppy being cast as an extra. While they're filming, Peppy keeps messing up and George just keeps playing along. George meets her in his dressing room and gives her a little pep talk on her acting career. After this, her career starts to soar from extras in his movies to even bigger parts. All is going great for them until one day when Peppy gets into a film with sound, or a "talkie". That is the day where everything turns around. George, being an expert silent actor and not letting go of his art, is fired from his current studio and forced to make his own living, but with the talkies being the new thing in Hollywood, his career starts to fall. Because of his pride in his art, his life starts to change drastically. It's an interesting plot idea executed artistically. 

ACTING:I mentioned before that acting in silent films has to be done carefully considering there's no dialogue. Well, the acting in here is brilliant for a modern-day silent film. Everybody did a pretty great job. Jean Dujardin played a brilliant and accurate role as George, capturing his laughs to his roles to his stresses. Berenice Bejo also played a well-done part as Peppy. I could really sense her feelings. The other shiners were John Goodman as Al Zimmer, Penelope Ann Miller as Doris, and Malcolm McDowell as the butler with honorable mentions to Bill Fagerbakke as the tuxedo policeman and the dog, Uggie, as himself. This animal was actually pretty well-trained. 

SCORE:The score was mainly made up of mood-fitting piano and string tunes that fit the era, plus a fitting song. I believe it was pretty well composed for a film of this type. 

OTHER CONTENT:This film was very well-made. It was charming in the same old way, visually pleasing in matching the time, and film with an artist's style and hand. I have to give credit to the director for filming this with such a vision and interest that it all comes together magically. The only problem I found with this is that for a silent film, it's too long. It starts to lag in the middle and lose a bit of its wonderful, nostalgic magic. I also kind of thought the character development had a flaw or two, but I just let it go. It was a worthy Oscar-winner, as "The King's Speech" was, but I believe there was a better of 2011. (HP7.2, Tree of Life) 

OVERALL,an awesome silent film with an interesting plot, brilliant silent acting, well-composed score, similar charm, pleasing visuals, and artistic execution, but it lags a bit in the middle and loses its nostalgic charm.

The Artist could have very easily gone the way of Soderbergh's "The Good German", as in being a film that was all style and zero substance. Thankfully, Michel Hazanavicius, Jean Dujardin and Berenice Bejo had something different in mind. They made, in 2011, a silent film that resonates. They made a film that said more with title cards than most films say with full-on dialogue. It's smart, funny, dramatic, and filled with incredible actors who can speak volumes with their facial expressions. It's a love-letter to a bygone era of filmmaking, but it also stands strong on its own merits. The Artist is a cinematic triumph.

The Artist is a perfect example of how an impeccable, charming style can make even the most ordinary movie seem phenomenal. At its' core, this is an ordinary "fall from grace / redemption" story as much as it is a love letter to the bygone days of silent cinema. The catch here is that it's presented as a (mostly) silent film, an approach that enhances the final product. The story, which centers on a silent film star resisting the progression towards "talkies", as the woman he loves becomes a massive star, is nothing we haven't seen before, but the way it's presented is new, innovative, and clever. Everything about the style-simplistic sets, the occasional sidestep to melodrama, a brilliant 1.33:1 AR, and a ridiculous adherence to retro framerate (22 FPS vs. 24) gives The Artist an authentic silent film feel. And, like many silent films, this one is jaunty and light, never delving (too far, anyway) into the more serious tropes of modern cinema. Oh, there are some dark themes peppered throughout (The fallacy of pride, self loathing, etc.) but the film's jaunty pace and general sense of delight ensure nothing ever gets too grim. The performances are uniformly excellent, primarily because, without words, the actors are required to communicate with their faces. Jean Dujardin may come across as annoyingly cheerful and peppy in interviews, but his persona REALLY works for this kind of movie; he does have a wonderfully expressive face. And it's so nice to see a movie where the score is a CHARACTER. The original score for The Artist is phenomenal, and, as is the case with many silent films, the music isn't simply there to enhance the scenes, but CONVEY THEM, which it does in spades. Did The Artist deserve all the accolades heaped upon it? Yes and no, I'd say. On one hand, the story is completely ordinary-a bit bland, I'd argue. On the other, this is a reminder that film can not only enhance even the simplest story, it can make such a story irresistible in the right hands. As a cinephile, I respect and applaud that message, and I'm glad somebody took the time to bring such a loving homage to the screen.

The Artist is, interestingly enough, unique because it takes advantage of several film techniques to develop its story but it's also not unique for the exact same reason.  For sure, the absence of diegetic sound and color makes it stand out over most, if not all, movies within the past few years.  However, the absence of a technique to convey a point is actually a familiar sight for those who know their movie history.  Schindler's List's and Pleasentville's purposeful absence of color utilizes the same type of philosophy that The Artist incorporates.  Remove a technique to convey a world as dramatically as possible only to fill in the technique when the character "completes his or her development" or when the plot concludes.  Upon further reflection, what The Artist did actually isn't really that original, but it did take it a step further than movies like Schindler's List or Pleasentville.  Film theory and comparisons aside, The Artist is a marvelous film on a very basic level.  It's a beautifully written, inspiring directed, and touchingly performed.  A silent film created in 2011 could easily become a gimmick that worn off after the midway point.  But, Michel Hazanavicius understands that the story should always comes first and the techniques and gimmicks of the movie ends up becoming a necessary part rather than a cheap play to be "artsy".  The Artist is a timeless and emotional story about being left behind by the world.  Whether, it's execution is actually novel will be left up to the film theorists to debate over, but the sincerity of the movie will be hard to deny.

The story is of a silent film actor named George Valentin. George is on top of the world, he is a superstar of the silent movie. After exiting a theater, George bumps into Peppy Miller. Peppy is an aspiring actress, and she soon gets a small part in one of George's movies. Peppy continues to have smaller roles in silent movies, but in 1929 Hollywood is switching to talkies. George thinks the idea is preposterous, and insists that silent movies are still superior. George leaves the Kinograph Studios when they switch to making talking movies, and finances, writes, directs, and stars in a new silent movie. Meanwhile, Peppy is becoming a huge star in the talking movie industry. The same day that George's silent movie is opening, Peppy's first talking movie is opening. Peppy's movie is a huge success, rocketing her into stardom, while George's movie fizzles. Then the Stock Market crashes, and George loses everything. The film continues with Peppy getting more and more popular, and George's life getting worse and worse.

French actor, Jean Dujardin, plays George. If you win an Oscar with only saying two words, well, that speaks strongly for itself. He is incredible as George. At the beginning of the movie, he has this confident bounce in his step of a man who has everything. But as the movie progresses, he must seem more and more miserable. This transformation must occur using only expressions. Dujardin is amazing. Also French actress, Berenice Bejo, plays Peppy. While I don't think her performance is as good as Dujardin's, she still must overcome the same problems as him in putting the performance on screen. She does a wonderful job as Peppy. Notable American actors, John Goodman and James Cromwell also star. They both knock it out of the park.

Overall, This movie is as sweet tribute to silent movies. What I hope it doesn't do is bring the genre back.  I can not say enough good things about this movie though. Ludovic Bource's score plays a big part, without it, the movie would be greatly diminished. Everything about this movie is done perfectly.

A homage to the retro classics and the silent movies of the 20th Century, The Artist is a formidable tribute to the most romantic period of the cinematographic history. Surprisingly gripping and charming this movie entertains not with special effects, cunning dialogues or modern glamor, but with the power of the cinema and the unforgettable smile of Jean Dujardin. 

As it could expected, the main story in The Artist is about the end of silent movies and the inevitable progress of the cinematography industry. In these changing times George Valentin (Jean Dujardin)is a famous actor who refuses to change, to embrace the cinematographic progress. He meets Peppy Miller (Bérénice Bejo), a young and ambitious  young lady who is climbing the Hollywood ladder and truly adores Valentin. Their story, the fall of Dujardin and the success of Bejo are told with emotions, with magic and wonderful music score.

Despite being a silent movie, the dramatic tension is built up step by step, and this without saying a single word. Indeed, Michel Hazanavicius' movie lacks the quality of narrative that some may have expected, but this is somehow compensated by the totally charming performance of Bejo and Dujardin. Speaking of the actors, Jean Dujardin and his smile are truly unforgettable. His self-assured and dramatic performance got him a most deserved Academy Award for Best Male Act and most of us are probably now curious to see how will his further career develop.

The Artist is a movie to enjoy, to embrace and to remember. It is that different movie which is released every year and differs from all other Hollywood deliveries. Yes, I may disagree with its Academy Award for Best Picture, but The Artist is surely a must see almost-classic !

The 2011 Academy Awards gave this film Best Picture. You can decide if it was well deserved or not.

It's told almost entirely as a black and white silent film with what would be considered over the top facial gestures (something that was really done in those days because there was no dialogue) with brief chatter on card shots and music to emphasize the various moods. It's a throwback to the glory days of silent film but also cleverly allows the viewer to experience an âupdatedâ? silent film. It's magical, dreamlike and sometimes even glorious in certain incidents (pay attention to the main character's pet dog, Ubbie) even if the story is overly predictable. I found the choice of music scores quite impressive.

George Valentin (Rudolph Valentino anyone?), our main character, played by actor Jean Dujardin is the ever popular charming yet arguably narcissistic lead man who refuses to accept that silent films are coming to an end. His love interest, Peppy Miller (played by Berenice Bejo), rises to fame as a star for the âtalkiesâ? while George's own stardom falls, leading to his depression, financial ruin and then possible renewal. 

The director has called this film a âlove letterâ? to the silent film cinema. Jean Dujardin picked up a well deserved Best Actor (you have to âgetâ? the silent film era to understand what a splendid job he did)  and is the first French actor to receive an Academy Award in that department. Incidentally, this is the first French film to win Best Picture as well (compare this picture to the previously nominated âLife is Beautifulâ? picture). Berenice Bejo is the oh so pretty love interest who intends to make it big and feels herself strongly drawn to the older male lead. Also starring John Goodman (the no nonsense studio boss), Malcolm McDowell (the butler), Penelope Ann Miller (George's irritating wife) and James Cromwell (the dutiful chauffeur).

This picture took roughly 35 days to film and was presented in the typical silent film 1:33:1 ratio. There are strong themes in this film about change and how those who don't change suffer yet those who adapt bounce back and sometimes do even better. It is also obviously a nostalgic look at an era long gone. People who enjoyed this film's focus on the loss of the silent film to âtalkiesâ? might also enjoy the 1950 âSunset Boulevardâ? as well as the 1937 âA Star is Bornâ? (which has a very similar story line to âThe Artistâ? though more bittersweet).

The budget for this film was only $15M yet it made over $133M at the Box Office. It garnered Best Director from the Academy Awards and was pretty much loved by almost all of the other critics and award givers.

Change.  Change is a big theme in THE ARTIST, as the film represents (in a fictitious manner) B&W silent films giving way to the advent of 'talkies' and as 'fresh meat' takes the place of the old.  In addition, THE ARTIST is a big change from what audiences see in theaters or at home in these times: an actual silent movie that utilizes its main actors top-notch talent of facially expressing their emotions minute-by-minute, second-by-second who are aided by classical movie-making visual flair and scene transitions.  

Featuring a French and American cast, THE ARTIST is filmed in traditional black and white, and that color palette suits the film's time period and the characters' personalities in a timely manner.  Jean Dujardin (say that name at least five times fast) stars as George Valentin, a big-time movie star of Pictograph Productions (with John Goodman as the CEO) who sees a downward spiral from fame and fortune to lost pride and poverty as 'talkies' take the place of the silent films he was crowned the king of.  Bérénice Bejo's Peppy Miller is given her first big break by Valentin in one of his pictures, and she goes on to become as famous as he is if not more.  

The emotions Valentin feels as Peppy Miller takes his place in the new format of films are jealousy, anger, pride, and regret.  Valentin undergoes a downward spiral of depression, loneliness, and a unhealthy sense of unhappiness as he lets his emotions run him and not his logic.  For the better portion of THE ARTIST's middle half, we see Valentin go from a smiling silent movie actor to a empty shadow of a man who literally has nothing more to lose.  While THE ARTIST is overall an upbeat film that presents as much joy and respect for the film industry as did HUGO, Valentin's struggle to change and to finally talk (in more ways than one) can be harrowing.  But the payoff is worth it.  

Every emotion felt in THE ARTIST can be attributed to the stars and to the two hidden stars of the film, the score and direction.  Written and directed by Michel Hazanavicius (the OSS 117 films), every classical movie technique and scene transitions of cinema's golden age can be seen in THE ARTIST.  Rise-to-fame montages, effective close-ups that utilize genuine emotion, the Iris Wipe, and many more make subtle (and noticeable to the trained eye) marks in THE ARTIST.  The composer did a terrific job as well.    

The format of chronicling one star's rise to fame and another's downfall is a story we've seen before, but what sets THE ARTIST apart from similar stories is the approach to silent/ talkie film techniques and to the genre's best virtues: genuine emotion and beautifully rendered visual palettes.  

THE ARTIST deserved the five Academy Award wins it earned, which included Best Picture.  For those who did not see THE ARTIST before the Academy Awards did not know what all the talk was about.  Now to the people who haven't seen THE ARTIST, it is a modern silent movie that utilizes the best virtues of the genre and a very evident theme of change that many audience members will find relevant to today's cinema as well as the times we live in.  Seeing the best that cinema has to offer can also allow us to see the best in ourselves, and perhaps that's why THE ARTIST is such an amazing film.

You will be aware every minute of the 100 minutes that 'The Artist' runs, of how romantically this film has been made. It is like the director is speaking to a lost love from a different era. And this, has very subtly been personified in the movie. This is what will stand out for me from the movie - Love. It portrays a different kind of love, distilled into its truest and purest form. The kind that isn't maligned with the selfish emotion of man. The kind that fills your heart with such warmth that you walk out of the theater with a big smile and feeling all fuzzy inside.

The scenes have been crafted with such perfection that you wonder if the director is really a magician. You applaud the details that have gone into painting every frame like it was a piece of historic art on the canvas, and the parallels that the movie has to offer. The specific scene where George Valentin discovers that he is still silent in a world that has begun to talk is a masterpiece. Or the scene where even his shadow abandons him. Or towards the end, when the movie literally ends with a 'Bang!'. Story-wise, it is gratifying that what happens on screen is what you expect to happen (in a restoring-faith-into-humanity sort of way).

The film succeeds on so many different levels, and considering that the film hardly had any words, that it is ironic how no number of words would be enough to describe the genius that this movie is. It even makes sense if you draw parallels with the state of contemporary cinema, where the major production houses have decided that "3D is the next big thing", and that "you will be left behind if you don't jump ships." Or man's path towards self-destruction. Or of melting pride and arrogance.

And boy can I speak enough about Jean Dujardin! What a controlled performance! I can see him transitioning to Hollywood soon enough, following the footsteps of Christoph Waltz. A truly well-deserved Oscar. (Although, my sympathies go out for George Clooney.)

I can understand if people would want to pass this movie - a black-and-white silent film, shot in 4:3 aspect ratio, with a lower framerate. Therefore, I strongly urge that you watch this film. It is a gem which, to watch in a theater is a privilege, and is the kind that succeeds in re-kindling the sublime romance that has been lost.

The Artist tells the tale of the film business moving from silent films to "talkies" through the character George Valentin. At the start of the movie, George is one of the biggest stars around. He's enjoying a flurry of success and is adored by all. He even meets a new woman Peppy Miller who stars in a movie with him. He met her in the street and was able to talk the executive into letting her appear in the movie. When they stop making silent films and only make "talkies", George is pushed aside for a new brand of filmmaking. A brand of filmmaking that makes the new, young, and beautiful Peppy Miller a star, and makes George Valentin a nobody.

This movies production values are amazing. The black and white cinematography is more than just beautiful. It also serves in taking us to the late 20's and early 30's. In 1927, famed silent film star George Valentin (Jean Dujardin) is on top of the world.  He's got a killer career, he's world famous, and he's got a loving wife and adorable dog.  Everything seems to be going for for him.

A chance encounter with wannabe star Peppy Miller (Bérénice Bejo) changes all that, and after she accidentally bumps into him on the red carpet, the press is all over her.  The era of silent films is dying, and is being replaced by talking pictures, with Peppy as its main star.

As her star rises, George's star falls, and he finds himself in squalor and debt, and is too prideful to accept Peppy's advice to move away from silent films and go to talking pictures.  As she keeps trying to be his guardian angel, George stumbles further and further into depression, and only once he lets go of his pride can he really come out of it.

Director Michel Hazanavicius brings forth a cinematic gem.  This is the first all silent, black-and-white film in decades (well, it's mostly silent, there's only a few words spoken at the end).  It brings back the limelight and wonder of old Hollywood, along with the glamorous costumes and spectacular talent.

Jean Dujardin and Bérénice Bejo give amazing performances because they couldn't rely on their voices, because their words are never heard.  Instead they have to rely on their physicality to tell the story, and they do so in spectacular fashion.  Dujardin deserved his Best Actor Oscar, and the film definitely deserved the Best Picture, Best Achievement in Costume Design, Best Achievement in Music Written for Motion Pictures, Original Score, and Best Director Oscars it also received.  If you're truly a fan of the cinema, this should top your list of must-see films.

After pushing a former nobody named Peppy Miller into the acting world, things regarding films begin to change.  Silent films are no longer acceptable.  Only films with talking can survive the box office now.  But George refuses to give in to "talkie" films.  So while George suffers, Peppy thrives.  And while Peppy only wants to be friends, George is determined to stay away from Peppy and talkie films.

Essentially, The Artist is riding on it's retro feel.  Everything from the visuals, to the costumes, to the score is all very retro and nostalgic.  And while this is The Artist's primary selling point, The Artist boasts many other attributes.

The story is not entirely original.  The apprentice surpassing the master, change, etc.  The Artist's story consists mostly of things we've seen before.  The trick, though, is that The Artist takes these worn elements in a whole new direction.  And of course, the old-fashioned feel helps with that.

The score (composed by Ludovic Bource) is much more important in this film than most others.  Due to the lack of dialogue and sound, the music is all you hear.  So if the music isn't fantastic the whole way through, it's up to the visuals to impress.  Thankfully, the music is not only good, it's superb.  With it's cheerful and old-fashioned feel, it's jazzy beats, and heavy (and appropriate) emphasis on the piano, The Artist's score is one the best of 2011.

Yet of course, The Artist won the Oscar for Best Original Score.  Frankly, it's hard to say whether it deserved it.  This is mostly because my other favorite scores of 2011 (Hugo and The Adventures of Tintin) are so distinctly different from the others, it's unfair to compare them.  Ultimately, the score for The Artist is the most broadly appealing, which boosted it's odds at winning (plus, the audience was paying more attention to the music, being a silent film).

This was a difficult role to play, but Dujardin nails it, and received a well-deserved Oscar for his efforts.  Berenice Bejo also does a fantastic job with her role as Peppy Miller, likewise for the rest of the cast.

Conveying gestures into understandable actions (with surprising minimal subtitles) was not an easy task, but the actors have accomplished this well.  Some scenes are so brilliantly acted and executed, they deserve a moment's appreciation.

Mixing drama with comedy, and adding some old school flair makes for a fresh and thoroughly entertaining film.  The Artist doesn't quite reach the dramatic heights that the Academy would like us to believe, but it comes close, and serves as a funny and moving depiction of accepting change.

If someone had told me at the beginning of 2011 that the best picture of the coming year would be a French-made tribute to silent era Hollywood, I never would have believed them. And if they said it would be a silent movie, I would have thought them quite mad. And I don't think I would have been alone. Which is why it's both a shock and a delight that for the first time since the inaugural Academy Awards, a silent film has swept the Oscars and become the toast of Hollywood.
	
And how could it not? It's the ultimate exercise in nostalgia, albeit for a time few if any of us are old enough to remember. It's a portal to a simpler, more innocent, and more glamorous time, even if that's only the way we remember it. It pays tribute to practically every genre of the time, from swashbucklers and safari flicks to high society romances and the dance numbers of Fred and Ginger.  True, its story of fading silent film star George Valentino and rising talkies actress Peppy Mills wouldn't have been all that original even then, yet that only adds to the timeless feel. Because the Artist doesn't hearken back to the silent era, it recreates it in near perfect detail.
	
The costumes, the sets, the title cards, all are all straight out of an old-timy two reeler. The dances are exactly as they were in the twenties. The musical score, heavy on jazz and vaudeville, sounds like it was penned in Tinpan Alley. Just like a real film from the period, the footage speeds up during tense or frantic scenes. The only clue that the Artist belongs to the twenty first century is that the picture quality is so high; lacking the graininess and occasional dark spots of the old celluloid reels.
	
 Even the cinematography seems to be from a bygone era, eschewing pans, tracking shots, and smooth transitions for the static camera shots and quick cuts that predominated at the time. Although this dedication to using period techniques does limit the variety of shots that can be used, the filmmakers compensate by filling the shots with movement and interaction between the actors. This is epitomized by a cutaway shot of the studio offices. As the protagonists briefly converse, dozens of figures pass them in every direction along two hallways and the wide staircase joining them.  With more movements than the eye can keep up with, the scene reminded me of the grand spectacles of Metropolis and Modern Times.
	
And the stars are simply wonderful. Their gestures are broad and exaggerated, their faces wonderfully expressive as they convey shock, anger, or sadness. With a hesitant smile or a smug lift of the chin they say nearly as much as they could by speaking. As George Valentino, Jean Dujardin bears an uncanny resemblance to Douglas Fairbanks, with just a touch of William Powell thrown in. At the beginning of the picture, he radiates strength, vitality, and the joy of a man doing what he loves. But as the years pass and his career fades, the lines on his brow multiply and his prominent chin seems to recede. It's almost like seeing Mark of Zorro and Prisoner of Zenda side by side.
	
Leading lady Bérénice Bejo doesn't strike a strong resemblance to any particular starlet of the period, but rather could pass for any young woman of the roaring twenties with her toothy grin, narrow hips, and flapper haircut. And of course the real star of this picture is Uggy, who may be the most photogenic canine since Nick and Nora's terrier Astra. His tricks are as impressive as any Lassie or Rin-Tin-Tin ever did, and even more adorable. I'm hopeful that this won't be his only role.

	Although it may not be the deepest or most complex of films, the Artist is surely among the most magical and delightful. Its attention to detail and love for its medium make it a treat for fans of the silent era, and its simplicity and sweetness will endear it even to those less familiar with the classics.. It would seem that this year in Hollywood, all that's old is new again.

The film is not entirely without charm, but is nothing more in the end than a gimmick movie featuring a generic love story with shallow characters. I respect the films that came before our current time, but that doesn't make this good on its own. This, for me, is the second-worst film (War Horse) nominated for best picture at this year's Academy Awards. Also, giving Jean Dujardin the Oscar just for acting as big as possible is absurd.

'The Artist,' much like Gene Kelly's 'Singin in the Rain,' is a film that serves as a reminder of the life of film before "talkies" and manages to poke playful fun at the silent film age. Unlike 'Singin in the Rain,' however, Michel Hazanavicius's picture takes ample time to pay homage to those films, and is itself a (mostly) silent movie.

'The Artist' follows the careers of two very different Hollywood Stars: George Valentin (Dujardin), a silent film actor nearing the end of his heyday, and young and spry Peppy Miller (Bejo), a young, up and coming actress who takes advantage of the revolution of talkie film-making. Throughout the story, Valentin's and Miller's lives criss-cross as the times of movies are a-changin;' Miller's career skyrockets while Valentin's spirals out of control. The way the plot climaxes with these two opposite lives is clever and quite satisfying.

Altogether, the story is a strong one that never forgets the humanity of its two leads, giving them plenty of time to grow and develop, and even manages to forgo what would at first glance seem like an obligatory, by-the-numbers romance. I wouldn't exactly call 'The Artist' a revolution in film-making nor the best picture of 2011, but it is a fun and admirable nod to the classic movies of the silent era.

An ode to silent films and the Golden Age of the Silver Screen, The Artist could easily become camp yet manages to rise above the novelty of black and white scenes, dialogue replaced by caption cards and a 4:3 aspect ratio. The film succeeds because it preserves the magic of Hollywood, not the techniques of 1920s filmmaking. Ultimately, the purpose of films is to entertain; silent films became obsolete when viewers wanted to see âtalkiesâ? and black and white films were replaced when colour was demanded. The Artist aspires to entertain the audience with a simple and charming story and elaborate effects are not necessary.

The plot is simple enough but serves a purpose to tell a deeper story about love and the worldâ(TM)s desire for entertainment. George Valentin is a leading silent film star and Peppy Miller is one of his adoring fans. Inspired by George, Peppy enters the movie industry and makes it big as George falls from grace. Although their careers are on opposite trajectories, the two remained infatuated with each other.

The screenplay is very funny; perhaps it is because the cards are used so sparingly that the writers can avoid the temptation to fill the silence with meaningless chatter. Since so few words are used, the actors must communicate their emotions through facial expressions and body language. As they fall out of fashion in The Artist, silent films are criticized because they force actors to emote instead of act. Stars Jean Dujardin and BÃ (C)rÃ (C)nice Bejo, supported by an ensemble cast featuring John Goodman and James Cromwell, show how skilled actors can draw in the audience and get their point across without many words.

Director Michel Hazanavicius should be commended for his creativity although he needed to produce a successful track record before studios would jump on board. With or without the silent film gimmicks, Hazanavicius puts the viewer in the protagonistâ(TM)s perspective: showcasing his arrogance and pride early in the film and his anger and desperation later. Valentin begins the film so incapable of interacting with others that he relates better to his dog and hallucinations that those around him. What a glorious movie this is! What a wonderful love letter to the cinema! And what a risk it was to make this film in the 21st century at a time when Hollywood studios would rather swim in safer waters then venture out and take a risk.  Here is a silent film, shot in gorgeous black and white that tells a familiar story, yet breaks free of gimmickry and becomes one of the most touching and magical films of the year.

Yes, the film is silent with the dialogue featured on title cards to tell us what the actors are saying, but this is something that we get comfortable with pretty quickly.  If you watch Turner Classic Movies late at night, you can probably catch a movie that looks something like this.  Anyone in love with old movies can quickly get into this story.

The story resembles most of the great epics about Hollywood, most especially A Star is Born, with a little of Singin' in the Rain and Sunset Blvd thrown in for good measure.  It begins in 1927, at a time when the art of the silent film was about the washed out by the advent of a new process called 'sound'.  Many of the biggest stars in motion pictures were about to have their careers obliterated by this new process, especially those who were middle aged - studios wanted young actors with young voices.

Standing at the precipice of this tidal wave of technology is George Valentin, a dashing romantic leading man whose fan-base mostly consists of giggling young girls (imagine Douglas Fairbanks and you've got the idea).  He is the star of a series of simple-minded action and romantic epics, usually featuring his trusty side-kick, an adorable and ever-faithful Terrier named Uggy.  George is happy in his life, although his wife self-centered wife Doris (Penelope Ann Miller) nags and complains that she's not only bored stiff, but uptight about his female admirers.  George is a very likable fellow, genial, funny, romantic, with a handsome face and a charming, ever-present smile.  He isn't smug at all.  He loves his fans and, near the film's opening, he spots a young wanna-be actress named Peppy Miller and touches her heart.  She is smitten by him, and it is difficult for him not to be smitten by her.  He gets her work, starting as an extra and, very quickly, her career is off and running.

The initial introduction to sound doesn't ruffle George at all. Cigar-chomping studio chief Al Zimmer (John Goodman) is convinced that this is the future, but George isn't too concerned. "If that's the future", he laughingly tells Zimmer, "You can have it!"  Soon, however, he finds that the process is no laughing matter and he is out of work.  Desperate to stay in the business, he makes a bold, and very foolish, move by financing a silent film himself with his own money. The product is silly adventure film that ends - prophetically - with George's character sinking into quicksand.

Financially ruined, George loses everything, Doris leaves him, and his only companions are Uggy, and his faithful driver Clifton (James Cromwell) who won't leave George's side even when he's been fired.  Meanwhile, the movie bombs, and ironically opens the same day as another picture, a romantic epic starring none-other than new star Peppy Miller.  His kindness to her comes back, as she tries to help him boost his defunct career.

The results of the story aren't exactly surprising to anyone familiar with the formula of most silent films.  What makes The Artist work is how much fun we have watching those old Hollywood movie conventions played out in fresh ways.  This is no stale recreation, writer-director Michel Hazanavicius turns his film into something truly special, playing with our perceptions and reminding us of a time when Hollywood movies had a dream-like quality, before "The Method", when the prepared theatricality of motion pictures made us feel as if we were stepping into another world.  He has fun with the over-dramatic moments that underline George's despair.  He even has fun with the title cards, especially during one crucial moment when we think that one thing has happened it turns out to be something else - you'll know the one I'm talking about.

Ever single facet of this film is extraordinary, from Guillaume Schiffman gorgeous black and white camera work, to Ludovic Bource' invaluable score that not-only punctuates the action but also touches our hearts at just the right moment.  The Art Direction by Gregory Hooper doesn't try to find a realistic note, but tries to make everything look and feel like a set.  And I must make mention of Mark Bridges' costumes, not only perfectly period, but perfectly luminous.

Yet, none of this would mean anything without the performances, especially by Jean Dujardin as George, a French actor that I am prevously unfamiliar with whose performance here got him the Best Actor prize at Cannes, the Golden Globe and The Oscar.  He looks and acts so much like a Hollywood leading man of the 1920's that we forget that this is a modern-day actor in his mid-30s.  He has a charm and a casual ease on the screen that makes us totally comfortable with him.  We like him, we care about him and he makes the movie work.

The other key to the film's success is Bérénice Bejo, as Peppy.  She has an open face and a smile that is three-feet wide.  She is charming in a way that reminds me a little of Janet Gaynor.  Lost in her love for George, her feelings for him are true and genuine.  Their chemistry together is something extraordinary.  There's not a moment that you can catch them with their guard down.

Movies like this are so rare.  They inform us of all the things that movies were made for, to transport us to another time and place, and to allow us to enter a dreamy world if only for a couple of hours.  The effect of this film on a true movie lover is not explained, it is only experienced.  How effective is it?  Let me put it this way: There is a moment early in the film, when Peppy enters alone into George's office. She finds his coat on a hanger. She slips her right arm into the empty left sleeve and wraps the arm around herself. George comes in and catches her. The two share a quiet romantic moment so tender and so touching that, I swear, it reminded of why I go to the movies.
